sections: Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
reqs: Explain why organizations adopt Six Sigma, how its philosophy and goals are applied, and how it grew out of the work of Juran, Deming, Shewhart, Ishikawa and other quality leaders.
Organizational goals and Six Sigma projects
Explain how a Six Sigma project is linked to and supported by organizational goals, write SMART goals, and describe how process inputs, outputs and feedback affect the whole organization.
Recognize the key business drivers for any type of organization and explain how KPIs, metrics and scorecards are developed and how they affect the organization.
Define and apply lean concepts including theory of constraints, value chain, flow, takt time, just-in-time, Gemba, spaghetti diagrams and perfection.
Value stream map and takt time
Use a value stream map to separate value-added steps from waste such as excess inventory, unused space, test inspection, rework, transportation and storage.
Value stream map and takt time
Distinguish DMADV from IDOV, relate both to DMAIC, explain how DfSS improves a product or process during design, and explain how verification and validation compare results with goals.
Basic failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA)
Use FMEA to identify failure modes, causes and effects, apply rating scales, calculate the RPN and analyze the results to set priorities.
Define design FMEA and process FMEA and apply the right one to a given situation.
Explain how projects are selected and when DMAIC fits better than another problem-solving approach.
Describe process components and boundaries and analyze the problems that arise when processes cross functions.
Distinguish competitive, collaborative and best-practice benchmarking and what each can deliver.
Identify input and output variables with a SIPOC and evaluate how inputs drive outputs.
Identify the process owner and the other stakeholders a project affects and engage them appropriately.
Identify a project's internal and external customers and judge how the project will affect them.
Voice of the customer to CTQ tree
Choose and apply surveys, focus groups, interviews and observation, and write data collection questions free of vagueness, ambiguity and bias.
Data collection plan and check sheet
Translate customer needs into features and measures with QFD, CTX, CTQ trees and the Kano model, weighting inputs by importance.
Voice of the customer to CTQ tree
Choose and apply agile or top-down project management to suit the project.
Describe charter elements and write a problem statement with baseline data and a measurable goal.
Help set project scope using process maps, Pareto charts and other quality tools.
Help define primary metrics for the goal and consequential metrics that guard against side effects.
Plan and monitor projects with WBS, Gantt charts, CPM, PERT and tollgate reviews.
Describe what a project must document and help build storyboards and summaries for reviews and updates.
Explain feasibility, impact, RPN and risk responses, and how risk can affect goals, resources, continuity, costs and stakeholders.
Close a project by reviewing results against the charter, storing documentation and sharing lessons learned.
Select and apply the seven management and planning tools and SWOT analysis.
Calculate DPU, RTY, CoPQ, DPMO, sigma level and capability indices and use them to drive project decisions.
Describe and use top-down, bottom-up and horizontal communication in organizations.
Describe the stages of team development and help resolve negative team dynamics.
Use RACI to define the roles of belts, champions, sponsors, executives, coaches, facilitators, members and process owners.
Apply brainstorming, nominal group technique and multivoting to generate and choose ideas.
Choose communication methods within the team and to stakeholders to report progress and run reviews.
Build process maps and review procedures, work instructions and flowcharts against how the work is really done to find gaps and misalignments.
Value stream map and takt time
Explain independent and mutually exclusive events, apply the multiplication rule, and count arrangements with permutations and combinations.
State the central limit theorem and explain why it lets us use normal-based confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and control charts for averages.
Describe the normal, binomial, Poisson, chi-square, t and F distributions and recognize where each applies in SPC and probability work.
Types of data and measurement scales
Classify data as continuous or discrete and as nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio, and judge what analysis each supports.
Data collection plan and check sheet
Sampling and data collection plans and methods
Choose random or stratified sampling, use check sheets and data coding, and write data collection plans that include data quality checks.
Data collection plan and check sheet
Calculate and interpret measures of center and spread and build frequency and cumulative frequency distributions.
Construct and read scatter diagrams, normal probability plots, histograms, stem-and-leaf plots and box plots.
Run and interpret gauge R&R, correlation, bias, linearity, attribute agreement and P/T studies to judge whether a measurement system is fit for use.
Tell natural process limits apart from specification limits and calculate performance metrics such as DPU, DPMO and yield.
Plan and run a capability study: pick the characteristic, confirm specifications and tolerances, and verify stability and normality before computing indices.
Process capability (Cp, Cpk) and process performance (Pp, Ppk) indices
Select and calculate Cp, Cpk, Pp, Ppk and Cpm, explain how they relate, and convert capability to a sigma level.
Short-term vs. long-term capability and sigma shift
Apply the conventions for short-term data and calculate the sigma shift between short-term and long-term performance.
Choose a sampling plan for a multi-vari study, build the chart, and read it to tell whether positional, cyclical or temporal variation dominates.
Tell correlation from causation, calculate and interpret the correlation coefficient and a simple linear regression with its p-value, and use the model to estimate and predict.
Separate statistical from practical significance, size samples, and set up tests with suitable significance level, power and type I and type II error risks.
Tests for means, variances, and proportions
Pick and run the right test (one- and two-sample t, paired t, F, ANOVA, proportions, chi-square) and interpret the result.
Describe the current and future states with the same predefined metrics and use the comparison to find and size performance gaps.
Value stream map and takt time
Use cause and effect diagrams, relational matrices, 5 Whys, fault tree analysis and similar tools to find and confirm the true cause of a problem.
Explain the core vocabulary of designed experiments, from factors, levels and responses to blocking, randomization, replication and effects.
Read main effects plots and interaction plots to judge which factors matter and whether the effect of one factor depends on another.
Plan how to put a solution in place by checking it first with proofs of concept, try-storming, simulations and pilot tests.
Choose and apply lean tools such as pull systems, kanban, 5S, standard work and poka-yoke to remove or prevent waste.
Analyze a process and cut its cycle time using continuous flow, setup reduction and SMED.
Value stream map and takt time
Tell ongoing kaizen apart from a kaizen blitz and pick the right one for a given situation.
Explain what SPC is for, how it monitors continuous and discrete process data, and tell common cause from special cause variation by reading a control chart.
Describe what a rational subgroup is and how subgroups and their timing are chosen so a control chart can separate within-subgroup and between-subgroup variation.
Choose the right variables or attribute control chart, calculate its limits, and use it to judge whether a process is in control.
Help build and put in place a control plan that documents how the improved process will be monitored and what to do when it goes wrong.
Explain how document control keeps only approved, current procedures in use and why that matters for holding the gains of a project.
Build training plans that bring people up to speed on an improved process and keep it running correctly over time.
Recognize first-, second- and third-party audits by who performs them and on whose behalf.
Tell the four PDCA steps apart and use the cycle to test, confirm and standardize an improvement.
Describe the elements of TPM, including predictive maintenance, and how they keep equipment able to hold an improved process.
Describe visual factory elements such as andon and jidoka and how they make abnormal conditions obvious so the improved process stays in control.
bank: I.A.1
Executives at a pump manufacturer are deciding whether to launch Six Sigma. Which reason best states its core business case?
It replaces the quality management system with a set of statistical tools
It moves responsibility for quality from operations to an inspection group
It lets the company match competitors' defect levels without changing processes
Reducing variation and defects lowers costs and raises customer satisfaction

Six Sigma pays off by reducing variation and defects, which cuts the cost of poor quality and improves what customers experience. It works inside a management system rather than replacing it, and it puts ownership on the process, not on inspectors.
std
I.A.1
A site leader says her plant now follows the Six Sigma philosophy. Which practice best supports that claim?
Experienced supervisors choose fixes quickly so that data collection does not slow things
Improvement targets are set at the current average so that they stay achievable
Defects are accepted as a normal cost and are covered through the rework budget
Process changes are approved only after data confirm the root cause they address
Six Sigma rests on data-driven decisions and fixing verified root causes. Relying on supervisor judgment alone skips the evidence that the philosophy demands.
std
I.A.1
Using the conventional 1.5 sigma long-term shift, a process operating at a six sigma level is expected to produce about how many defects per million opportunities?

Six sigma with the 1.5 sigma shift leaves 4.5 sigma to the nearer limit, about 3.4 DPMO. The figure 0.002 is the two-sided value with no shift, and 233 and 6,210 correspond to five and four sigma with the shift.
std
I.A.1
A quality director organizes all quality work as planning, control and improvement, and insists that improvement happen project by project. Whose approach is she following?
W. Edwards Deming
Philip Crosby
Joseph Juran
Kaoru Ishikawa

The quality trilogy and project-by-project improvement are Juran's ideas, and Six Sigma's project structure owes much to them. Deming is known for the 14 points and the system of profound knowledge, not the trilogy.
std
I.A.1
After a jump in defects, a plant manager posts banners urging operators to work more carefully. Which response reflects Deming's view?
Slogans work well when paired with individual bonuses tied to each operator's defect count
Most problems come from the system, which management must fix, so slogans will not help
Operators should be retrained in final inspection so that they catch defects before shipment
Defects should be budgeted as a cost of quality and tracked in a monthly management report

Deming held that most variation is built into the system and that exhortations aimed at the workforce only frustrate people. Tying bonuses to individual defect counts runs against his call to remove numerical quotas and fear.
std
I.A.1
Six Sigma's use of control charts to separate common-cause from assignable-cause variation traces most directly to whose work?
Kaoru Ishikawa's quality circle movement in postwar Japan
Walter Shewhart's work at Bell Telephone Laboratories
Philip Crosby's zero defects program in the aerospace industry
Joseph Juran's application of the Pareto principle to quality

Shewhart developed the control chart and the idea of chance versus assignable causes at Bell Labs. Juran's Pareto work concerns separating the vital few problems from the trivial many, not process variation over time.
std
I.A.1

A team builds a cause-and-effect diagram, and the company trains front-line workers in the basic quality tools so they can solve problems in small groups. Which quality leader is most associated with both practices?
Kaoru Ishikawa
Walter Shewhart
Joseph Juran
Armand Feigenbaum

Ishikawa created the cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagram and championed the basic tools and quality circles for front-line workers. Feigenbaum is known for total quality control, not these worker-level tools.
std
I.A.1
Which statement best describes how Six Sigma emerged as a named methodology?
Deming created it in postwar Japan to replace statistical process control charts
Motorola developed it in the 1980s, building on earlier statistical quality work
It began as a military sampling standard used to accept incoming material lots
Shewhart introduced it as a rule for placing control limits six sigmas apart

Six Sigma was developed at Motorola in the mid-1980s and later spread widely through industry, drawing on the work of earlier quality leaders. Deming did not create it, and control chart limits are set at three sigmas, not six.
std
I.A.1

A consultant tells executives that quality means conformance to requirements, that the performance standard is zero defects, and that quality should be measured by the price of nonconformance. Whose ideas is she presenting?
Philip Crosby
Joseph Juran
Walter Shewhart
Genichi Taguchi
Conformance to requirements, zero defects and the price of nonconformance are Crosby's hallmark ideas. Juran defined quality as fitness for use, which differs from Crosby's conformance view.
std
I.A.2

A champion is choosing among candidate projects. This year's strategic plan includes an objective to raise customer loyalty on the commercial product line. Which project shows the strongest link to organizational goals?
Fixing a process a supervisor proposed because it has long frustrated her team on night shift
Studying a process chosen because the team already has data on hand and could finish quickly
Cutting warranty returns on commercial units, named in the loyalty objective as a key complaint
Trying out a new statistical tool that the Black Belt recently learned about in advanced training

A project should connect directly to a stated organizational goal so that its results matter to leaders and earn support. A project chosen for convenience or available data may be easy, but it has no tie to strategy.
std
I.A.2
A Green Belt project aligned with a plant goal on delivery is stalled because the team cannot get time on a test machine. Which support should have been set up when the project was launched?
A rule that the team reports progress to managers only at the end of the project
A team made up entirely of volunteers so that managers stay out of the work
A sponsor who owns the goal and can supply resources and remove barriers
A budget drawn only from the quality department's discretionary spending

Linking a project to a goal is not enough; a sponsor or champion with authority over the goal secures resources and clears obstacles like this one. Reporting only at the end hides the problem from the people who could solve it.
std
I.A.2
Which project goal is written in SMART form?
Reduce invoice errors at the billing center from 4.2% to 1.5% by June 30
Significantly improve invoice accuracy at the billing center during this year
Make invoice errors at the billing center as rare as those of the best competitor
Cut invoice errors to 1.5% by focusing the billing team on accuracy and care
The key states what will change, a measurable baseline and target, and a deadline, and the target is a realistic reduction. The last option has a target but no date, so it is not time-bound.
std
I.A.2
A molding process runs at 8% scrap. The sponsor writes the goal: "Reduce scrap on line 4 to 0% by the end of next month." Which SMART element is weakest?
Specific
Measurable
Achievable
Time-bound
The goal names the line, a measurable target and a date, but going from 8% to zero in a month is not realistic. It is specific and measurable, so those are not the weak points.
std
I.A.2
A molding team switches to a cheaper resin. Its own yield is unchanged, but the downstream assembly area begins finding more cracked housings. What does this show most clearly?
Outputs of one process are inputs to another, so local changes must be judged by system-wide effects
The assembly process is now out of control and should be the subject of a separate Six Sigma project
The molding team's steady yield shows the resin change was sound and should be kept in place
Downstream defects should be charged back to the resin supplier under the purchasing agreement

A change in an input can pass through one process's outputs and cause problems further along, even when local measures look fine. Launching a separate project in assembly treats the symptom and ignores the upstream cause.
std
I.A.2
A plant wants feedback from its processes to influence decisions across the organization. Which arrangement best does this?
All process data go to the quality department, which issues one summary report each year
Operators hear about results only when a customer complaint names their particular area
Leaders get raw readings from every machine each day so they can direct the adjustments
Operators see results hourly, managers see weekly trends, and leaders see monthly goal results

Feedback works when each level gets information at the frequency and detail it needs to act. Sending raw machine data to leaders overloads them and takes routine adjustment away from the people closest to the process.
std
I.A.2
A call center's customers report that answers to billing questions are often wrong. Agents never hear about these reports, which go only to the marketing department. What is the main problem?
Marketing should be the owner of billing accuracy because it receives the customer reports
The feedback never reaches the agents whose process creates the errors, so nothing is corrected
The center needs more agents so each of them has extra time to research every billing question
Customers should be asked to send complaints by letter so that a formal record exists for each
Feedback is only useful if it reaches the people and process that can act on it. Making marketing the owner keeps the information away from the agents who generate the errors.
std
I.A.3
A Green Belt project cuts scrap cost by $200,000 a year with no change in selling price or sales volume. Which business driver does it affect most directly?
Profit
Market share
Product differentiation
Customer satisfaction
Lower cost at the same revenue goes straight to profit. Market share would change only if sales volume changed relative to the market, which it did not.
std
I.A.3
A company's sales rose 10% last year while the total market for its products grew 25%. What happened to its market share?
It fell, because sales grew more slowly than the market
It rose, because the company's sales went up during the year
It stayed the same, because both sales and the market increased
It cannot be judged without knowing the company's profit margin
Market share is company sales divided by total market sales; 1.10 divided by 1.25 is 0.88, so share dropped by about 12% of its former value. Rising sales alone do not mean rising share.
std
I.A.3
A service firm's revenue is steady, but its repeat-customer rate has dropped and complaints are rising. Which business driver is giving the earliest warning?
Profit, because revenue is the first figure to show customer discontent
Customer satisfaction, which tends to move before retention and revenue
Market share, because complaints show that competitors are cutting prices
Product differentiation, because repeat rates depend mainly on new features
Falling repeat business and rising complaints signal weakening customer satisfaction, which usually shows up before revenue drops. Revenue is a lagging measure, which is why it is still steady here.
std
I.A.3
A distribution center ships the same volume with 15% fewer labor hours and no change in error rate. Which business driver improved?
Market share
Efficiency
Product differentiation
Customer satisfaction
The same output from fewer inputs is a gain in efficiency. Customer satisfaction would be expected to change only if service to customers changed, and errors stayed flat.
std
I.A.3
A power tool maker sells a battery platform no competitor can match and charges a premium price for it. Which business driver does this strategy rely on most?
Efficiency in production
Lower cost of quality
Product differentiation
Market share from discounts
Competing on unique features that justify a higher price is product differentiation. Efficiency and cost reduction support a low-cost strategy, not a premium one.
std
I.A.3
What sets a key performance indicator (KPI) apart from the many other metrics a department tracks?
It is reported more often than any other measure in the department
It is picked by each department without regard to company strategy
It measures something critical to an organizational goal
It is stated in dollars so that departments can compare their results
A KPI is a measure selected because it reflects progress on a goal that matters to the organization's success. Reporting frequency or currency units do not make a metric key.
std
I.A.3
A nonprofit food bank wants business drivers to guide its improvement work. Which pair of measures fits best?
Return on equity and growth in the share price over peers
Number of new staff hired and size of the office space used
Meals delivered per dollar donated and client satisfaction
Gross profit margin and the volume of food items purchased

Every organization has drivers; for a nonprofit they center on mission delivery, efficient use of funds and the satisfaction of those it serves. Equity returns and share price apply to investor-owned companies, not a food bank.
std
I.A.3
A business unit is building a balanced scorecard. Which step should come first?
List every metric departments already collect and sort them into the four perspectives
Set financial targets first and add the other perspectives only if time and data allow
Translate strategy into objectives for each perspective, then choose measures for those
Ask each department to design its own scorecard independently of the other departments

A scorecard should start from strategy: objectives come first, and measures are chosen to track them across the financial, customer, internal process, and learning and growth perspectives. Sorting existing metrics into boxes produces a list, not a strategy-linked scorecard.
std
I.A.3
A scorecard team wants a leading indicator to go with its lagging measure of annual customer retention. Which measure fits best?
Revenue from repeat customers over the past fiscal year
Share of customer complaints resolved within 48 hours
Customer churn rate reported at the end of last year
Year-end market share figure from the industry report
Complaint resolution speed changes before customers decide whether to stay, so it gives early warning. The other measures report outcomes after the fact and are lagging indicators.
std
I.A.3
A call center rewards agents for short average call times. Calls get shorter, but repeat calls and complaints rise. What does this show?
Agents need more training on the call script before the metric can be judged properly
Metrics drive behavior, so one narrow measure can work against the wider business goals
The call-time target was set too loosely to change agents' behavior in a useful way
Call time should be reported weekly rather than daily to smooth out the variation
People optimize what they are measured on, and a narrow metric can improve locally while customers and the business suffer. The target clearly did change behavior, so it was not too loose.
std
I.A.3
How should a plant's scorecard relate to the corporate scorecard?
Plant measures should be chosen locally so that the plant keeps control of its priorities
The plant should copy the corporate measures exactly without adapting them to operations
The plant should track only financial measures, since corporate handles the other areas
Plant measures should be derived from corporate objectives so that local results roll up

Cascading objectives aligns each level's measures with company goals, so local improvement adds up to corporate results. Copying corporate measures without translation leaves people without measures they can influence.
std
I.B.1
A line runs two 8-hour shifts a day, and each shift has 30 minutes of planned breaks. Customer demand is 450 units a day. What is the takt time?
128 seconds
60 seconds
240 seconds
120 seconds
Available time is 2 × (480 − 30) = 900 minutes, or 54,000 seconds; 54,000 / 450 = 120 seconds. Leaving the breaks in gives 128 seconds, which overstates the time available.
std
I.B.1
Takt time on an assembly line is 120 seconds. One station has a cycle time of 140 seconds. What does this mean?
The station has spare capacity and could take on work from neighboring stations
Takt time should be raised to 140 seconds so that it matches the station's pace
The station cannot keep pace with demand and needs rebalancing or more capacity
The line is producing ahead of demand and will build excess finished goods
A cycle time longer than takt means the station cannot produce at the rate customers need. Takt time is set by demand, so it cannot be raised just to match a slow station.
std
I.B.1
Using the theory of constraints, a team has identified a heat-treat oven as the plant's bottleneck. What should it do next?
Elevate the oven by buying a second one to double its capacity
Raise the output of every other operation to its maximum rate
Move the focus to the next slowest operation in the plant
Exploit it by getting the most from it with existing resources

After identifying the constraint, the next step is to exploit it, for example by eliminating idle time and running only good parts through it. Buying capacity is the elevate step, which comes only after exploiting and subordinating.
std
I.B.1
A team cuts the cycle time of a machine that is not the plant's constraint by 20%. What effect on plant throughput should it expect?
About a 20% increase, matching the cycle time reduction
A decrease, because the machine will now starve upstream
An increase equal to the constraint's idle time each shift
Little or none, because the constraint limits output

Throughput of the whole system is set by its constraint, so speeding up a non-constraint mainly adds inventory in front of the bottleneck. Expecting a matching 20% gain ignores where the limit actually is.
std
I.B.1
In Porter's value chain, which activity is classed as a support activity rather than a primary activity?
Human resource management
Outbound logistics
Marketing and sales
After-sale service

Support activities include firm infrastructure, human resource management, technology development and procurement. Outbound logistics, marketing and sales, and service are primary activities that directly create and deliver the product.
std
I.B.1
A machining cell builds parts in batches of 50 and moves each batch together to the next step. What is the main benefit of changing to one-piece flow?
Each machine's utilization rises because it stays busy for longer stretches of time
Lead time drops and defects surface sooner, since each part moves on when it is done
Inventory between steps grows, which protects output against equipment breakdowns
Takt time drops because customer demand rises once lead time becomes shorter

Moving parts one at a time removes the wait for the rest of the batch, cutting lead time and letting a defect be caught after one part instead of fifty. Flow aims to reduce inventory between steps, not increase it.
std
I.B.1
Which practice is most consistent with just-in-time production?
Products are built to a monthly forecast and kept in finished goods until orders arrive
Material is bought in large lots for volume discounts and backed by generous safety stock
Each machine runs at its full rate so that hourly output is as high as possible
A kanban card signals the upstream cell to make parts only after downstream uses them
JIT makes what is needed, when it is needed, in the amount needed, and kanban pull is a standard way to do it. Building to forecast and holding stock is the push approach JIT is meant to replace.
std
I.B.1
A Green Belt learns that scrap at a stamping press has doubled this month. Which first step best reflects the Gemba principle?
Pull a month of scrap reports and study them at her desk for patterns
Gather supervisors in a conference room to brainstorm likely causes
Send operators a survey asking what they think is going wrong
Go to the press to watch the process and talk with operators
Gemba means going to the actual place where the work happens to see the facts firsthand. Reviewing reports at a desk relies on secondhand data and misses what is happening at the press.
std
I.B.1
A team traces a nurse's movements on a floor plan of a hospital ward over one shift. What is the drawing most useful for?
Measuring variation in the times medications are given
Calculating takt time for admissions to the ward
Revealing excess walking caused by the layout
Ranking the causes of patient complaints by frequency
A spaghetti diagram maps the actual path of people or material so that wasted motion and transport stand out. It shows paths, not timing data, so it cannot measure dosing time variation.
std
I.B.1
In lean thinking, what does the principle of perfection mean?
Reaching zero defects once and then freezing the process to hold that level
Inspecting each unit so that no defect can reach the customer at all
Setting stretch targets that teams are expected to meet within one year
Removing waste continually so that value flows with ever less effort and cost

Perfection is the final lean principle: after specifying value, mapping the stream, creating flow and pull, the organization keeps cycling through improvement indefinitely. Freezing the process treats improvement as a one-time event, which is the opposite idea.
std
I.B.2
On a current-state value stream map for a valve body, which step is value-added?
Moving parts by forklift to the next cell
Checking the bore with a plug gauge
Storing finished parts until shipment
Machining the bore to its final size
A value-added step changes the product in a way the customer will pay for and is done right the first time. Gauging confirms the bore but does not change it, so it is not value-added.
std
I.B.2
A value stream map shows 12 minutes of value-added time and a total lead time of 2,400 minutes. What is the process cycle efficiency?
Process cycle efficiency is value-added time divided by lead time: 12 / 2,400 = 0.005, or 0.5%. A result of 5% comes from misplacing the decimal point.
std
I.B.2
A value stream map shows 900 units of work in process between two steps. Customer demand is 300 units a day. Using Little's law, how much lead time does this inventory add?
3 days
0.33 day
1.5 days
6 days
Lead time equals inventory divided by the daily demand rate: 900 / 300 = 3 days. Dividing demand by inventory gives 0.33, which inverts the relationship.
std
I.B.2
A team's value stream map shows large piles of work in process between every pair of steps. Besides adding lead time, why is this excess inventory treated as waste?
It is value-added because it protects the line from breakdowns
It reduces handling because parts are moved less often in total
It ties up cash and hides problems such as defects and imbalance
It shortens takt time because more parts are ready to be used

Excess inventory costs money to hold and masks problems, so defects and imbalances go unnoticed until much later. Calling it value-added confuses a buffer against problems with something the customer pays for.
std
I.B.2
During a value stream walk, a team finds a mezzanine filled with idle equipment and empty racks. Why should it note this on the map?
Idle space still costs rent, utilities and upkeep, and it could host value-adding work instead
Floor space has no effect on the value stream, so the note is only for the facilities group
Idle equipment can be counted as spare capacity and added to the cycle time data box
Empty racks show the plant is running lean and should be recorded as a best practice

Space that does nothing still costs money and often hides other waste, so it belongs on the map as an improvement opportunity. It is not neutral to the value stream, because the cost is borne by the products that flow through it.
std
I.B.2
A product goes through a 100% functional test at the end of the line, which catches about 3% failures. How should the team classify this step on its value stream map?
Value-added, since it raises the quality of the product that the customer receives
Storage, since units wait in a queue for the test station before being tested
Not a process step, so it should be left off the map and handled separately
Non-value-added, since it does not change the product even if it is needed for now
Test and inspection do not transform the product, so they are non-value-added, even when they are needed today to protect the customer. Testing finds defects but does not add quality to good units.
std
I.B.2
A value stream map shows that 12% of units loop back from final assembly to a rework bench. How should the team view this loop?
As a value-added step, because rework turns a defective unit into a good one
As waste that uses capacity and adds handling time and lead time to the flow
As a normal cost that should be left off the map because it is not planned
As inspection, because the rework bench checks each unit before it returns

Rework repeats work that should have been done right the first time, so it consumes capacity and lengthens lead time without adding value. Fixing a defect only restores what the customer already expected, so it is not value-added.
std
I.B.2
A value stream map shows parts traveling 400 meters by forklift between two cells that run in sequence. Which future-state change best removes this waste?
Relocate the cells next to each other so that parts pass directly between them
Buy a faster forklift so that each trip between the two cells takes less time
Increase the batch size so that fewer forklift trips are needed during a shift
Add a staging area at each end of the route to hold parts waiting for a trip
Removing the distance removes the transportation waste rather than just speeding it up. Larger batches reduce trips but add inventory and lead time, trading one waste for another.
std
I.B.2
A value stream map shows that raw material sits in a warehouse for an average of 20 days before it is used. How should the team treat this?
As a value-added step, because the material is being kept safe until needed
As storage waste that adds lead time and carrying cost without adding value
As a necessary step that should not be challenged, since stock is a supplier issue
As transportation waste, because material must be moved into the warehouse
Material sitting in storage adds days to lead time and costs money to hold, with nothing done to it. Moving material into the warehouse is transportation, but the 20 days of waiting is storage.
std
I.C.1
When is DMADV a better choice than DMAIC?
When a new product is needed or an existing one cannot be improved enough to meet requirements
When a stable process has a known root cause and needs a quick fix within a few weeks
When the team wants to skip data collection so that the project can finish sooner
When a process is capable and in control but managers want better documentation of it
DMADV is used to design something new or to redesign a process that improvement alone cannot bring up to requirements. A known root cause in an existing process is a job for DMAIC or a simpler fix.
std
I.C.1
Which DMADV phase takes the place of the Improve phase in DMAIC?
Define
Verify
Analyze
Design
Define, Measure and Analyze appear in both road maps; Design replaces Improve, and Verify replaces Control. Verify is the counterpart of Control, not Improve.
std
I.C.1
In the IDOV road map, what is the Optimize phase mainly used for?
Tuning parameters and tolerances so the design is capable and robust
Gathering customer needs and turning them into critical-to-quality requirements
Confirming through pilot runs that the finished design meets its requirements
Writing the business case and charter that justify starting the design project
Optimize refines the chosen design, often with robust design and tolerance analysis, so it performs well despite variation. Pilot confirmation belongs to Verify, the last phase.
std
I.C.1
In the IDOV road map, what work is done in the Identify phase?
Defining the project and translating customer needs into CTQ requirements
Choosing among design concepts and building the selected detailed design
Setting tolerances that make the design robust against sources of variation
Running pilot builds to confirm the design meets its stated requirements

Identify sets up the project and captures customer requirements as measurable CTQs, roughly covering DMAIC's Define and Measure. Concept selection and detailed design happen in the Design phase that follows.
std
I.C.1
Why does an organization apply DfSS during product design instead of relying on DMAIC projects after launch?
DMAIC cannot be applied to any process that makes a product introduced in the past few years
Design choices set much of a product's cost and quality, so prevention there costs less
DfSS lets the team skip customer research because the design is based on engineering data
Products designed with DfSS do not need verification or validation before they are released

Design decisions lock in most of a product's cost and its capability, and changes become far more expensive after launch. DfSS still begins with the voice of the customer, so skipping customer research contradicts it.
std
I.C.1
Engineers test prototypes of a new valve and confirm that each one withstands the 300 psi burst pressure stated in the design input requirements. What activity is this?
Design validation
Process validation
Design verification
Design review

Verification confirms that design outputs meet the specified design inputs, which is what the burst test checks. Validation asks whether the product meets the user's needs in its intended use, which a bench test against a spec does not show.
std
I.C.1

A design team gives prototype sprayers to growers, who use them on their own fields for a season. The team then compares the results with the goals in its charter for coverage and ease of use. What activity is this?
Design verification
Gauge calibration
Final inspection
Design validation

Validation confirms that the product meets user needs in its intended use, which a field trial under real conditions shows. Verification compares outputs with written specifications in controlled tests, not with users in real conditions.
std
I.C.2
An FMEA team rates a failure mode with severity 7, occurrence 4 and detection 5. What is the risk priority number?
RPN is severity × occurrence × detection: 7 × 4 × 5 = 140. Adding the ratings gives 16, a common slip.
std
I.C.2

A team's severity scale defines 9 as a safety hazard to the user. Its FMEA shows: mode A, S = 9, O = 2, D = 3; mode B, S = 4, O = 6, D = 5; mode C, S = 3, O = 5, D = 6. Which mode should get attention first?
Mode B, because its RPN of 120 is the highest of the three failure modes
Mode C, because its detection rating of 6 is the worst among the three modes
Mode B, because its occurrence of 6 means it fails most often
Mode A, because a safety-level severity needs action whatever its RPN
Mode A's RPN is only 54, but a safety-level severity is normally addressed first whatever the RPN. Ranking by RPN alone would put B (120) first, which ignores that a low RPN can hide a severe effect.
std
I.C.2
On a typical FMEA detection scale, what does a rating of 10 mean?
Current controls are almost certain to detect the failure
The failure is expected to occur very frequently
Current controls will almost surely miss the failure
The effect is hazardous and occurs without warning

Detection is rated in reverse: higher numbers mean a lower chance of catching the failure, so 10 is the worst case. A hazardous effect without warning describes the top of the severity scale, not detection.
std
I.C.2
FMEA team members disagree on occurrence ratings because each of them reads "moderate" differently. What is the best fix?
Define the scale with criteria tied to failure rates and apply it consistently
Average each member's rating so that every opinion is reflected in the final number
Have the most senior engineer assign all ratings to settle the disagreement quickly
Drop occurrence from the analysis and calculate risk from severity and detection

Clear scale criteria, ideally linked to data such as failure rates, make ratings consistent and comparable. Averaging opinions hides the disagreement without giving anyone a shared basis for the ratings.
std
I.C.2
A team adds an automated end-of-line test that catches a failure mode it had rated S = 8, O = 5, D = 7. Which rating should change?
Severity, because the customer is now better protected
Detection only; severity and occurrence stay the same
Occurrence, because fewer failures will now take place
All three ratings, because the overall risk has gone down
A new detection control improves the chance of catching the failure, so only the detection rating drops. It does not stop the failure from happening or make its effect less severe if it does occur.
std
I.C.2
In an FMEA for a coffee maker, the failure mode is "heating element does not switch off." Which entry belongs in the effect column?
Water boils dry and the housing overheats
Thermostat contacts weld together and stick
Thermal cutoff is tested at the end of the line
Specify a thermostat with a higher contact rating
An effect is the consequence of the failure as the user or next process experiences it. Welded thermostat contacts would cause the failure mode, so that entry belongs in the cause column.
std
I.C.2
In an FMEA for a bolted joint, the failure mode is "joint loosens in service." Which entry is a potential cause?
Torque tool set below the specified value
Customer hears rattling and returns the unit
Torque is audited at the start of each shift
Severity is rated 7 for this failure mode
A cause is what makes the failure mode happen, and low applied torque does that. The rattle and return describe the effect, which is what the customer experiences after the joint loosens.
std
I.C.2
A team installs error-proofing that physically prevents the cause of its top-ranked failure mode. What should it do next in the FMEA?
Close the line item, because a completed action means the risk is fully removed
Lower the severity rating, since the error-proofing protects the customer
Revise the ratings, recalculate the RPN and confirm the risk has dropped
Move on to the next failure mode and leave the original ratings in place

An FMEA is a living document: after actions are taken, the ratings are revised and the new RPN is checked to confirm the expected reduction. Prevention lowers occurrence, not severity, because the effect would be just as serious if the failure did happen.
std
I.C.3
A team studies how a bracket with its specified wall thickness could crack under the rated load in service. Which tool are they using?
Process FMEA
Design FMEA
Control plan
Capability study
Looking at how the design itself could fail in use is a design FMEA. A process FMEA would look at how manufacturing could fail to make the bracket as designed.
std
I.C.3
A team lists ways a welding station could produce porous welds, such as wrong shielding gas flow or contaminated wire. Which tool are they using?
Design FMEA
Design review
Process FMEA
Fault tree analysis

Failures that the manufacturing process introduces, with causes such as gas flow and wire condition, are the subject of a process FMEA. A design FMEA would assume the part is built to print and ask whether the design itself is adequate.
std
I.C.3
When preparing a process FMEA, how should the team treat the product design?
Reassess the design margins of every feature before listing any process failures
Assume the design meets its intent and focus on failures the process could add
Leave severity ratings blank until the design FMEA has been fully repeated
Record any design weaknesses that are found as causes in the process FMEA

A process FMEA assumes the design is sound and analyzes how manufacturing or assembly could fail to deliver it. Design weaknesses that turn up should be fed back to the design FMEA, not recorded as process causes.
std
I.C.3
Which control would normally appear in a design FMEA rather than a process FMEA?
Control charts on a critical dimension at the machining cell
A fixture that stops a part from being loaded backward
Durability testing of prototypes to confirm the design life
Visual checks by the operator at each assembly station

Design controls verify that the design will meet its requirements, and prototype durability testing does that. A fixture that prevents wrong loading is error-proofing in the manufacturing process, so it belongs in a process FMEA.
std
I.C.3

A design FMEA rates the end effect "seal leaks and fluid is lost" at severity 8. The process FMEA lists a press-fit step that could cause the same leak. How should severity be set for that process failure?
Use the same severity of 8, because the end effect on the customer is the same
Rate severity lower, because process controls already reduce how often it occurs
Rate severity from scratch, because the two FMEAs are not meant to be linked
Leave severity out, because a process FMEA rates only occurrence and detection

Severity depends on the effect, so the same end effect should carry the same rating across the linked FMEAs. Occurrence reflects frequency; controls that make the failure less frequent do not change how serious its effect is.
std
II.A.1
A conveyor keeps jamming because a guide rail is visibly worn. Maintenance agrees that replacing the rail will fix it. A supervisor asks for a Six Sigma project. What is the best response?
Replace the rail as a just-do-it fix and confirm the jams stop
Launch a full DMAIC project so the fix is backed by baseline data
Run a designed experiment to prove the rail is the true cause
Assign the jam to a black belt as a multi-phase project
DMAIC is meant for problems whose cause or solution is unknown; when both are obvious, the quick fix is the right path. A full project here spends weeks proving what everyone already knows.
std
II.A.1
Which situation is best suited to the DMAIC methodology?
A new product must be designed for a market the company has never served
An existing process has chronic, measurable variation and the cause is not known
A chemical spill on the floor needs to be contained in the next hour
The cause of a problem is known and the fix only needs funding

DMAIC improves existing processes where data can be gathered and the cause is not yet understood. A brand-new design calls for a design approach such as DMADV, and an emergency needs immediate containment rather than a project.
std
II.A.1
A steering committee has twelve candidate projects and can staff only four. Which basis for choosing is best?
Fund the projects proposed by the most senior managers in the business
Fund the four quickest projects regardless of their expected benefit
Fund the four broadest projects because they promise the largest savings
Rate each on strategic fit, benefit, resources and odds of success

Project selection should weigh benefit, alignment with goals, required resources and likelihood of success together. Picking the broadest projects is tempting, but broad scope is a common reason projects stall and fail to deliver.
std
II.A.1
A candidate project promises large savings on a packing line. The plant plans to replace that line with an automated cell in five months. What is the main concern in selecting it?
The project will need more than one green belt to complete on time
The benefits may never be realized because the process is being replaced
Packing lines rarely produce enough data for a capability study
The savings estimate must first be confirmed by an outside auditor
Selection considers whether the benefit will last; improving a process that is about to disappear wastes the effort. The staffing and data points are minor by comparison and can be managed.
std
II.A.1
A team has a recurring defect, a cause that is unknown, and a process that can be measured, but the issue is small and confined to one workstation. Which approach is usually most practical?
A full DMAIC project chartered and reviewed by the executive council
A DFSS project to redesign the product from the ground up
A short PDCA or kaizen effort by the people who run the workstation
No action until the defect grows large enough to justify DMAIC

Not every problem needs full DMAIC; small, local problems with modest stakes are often solved faster with simpler problem-solving cycles. Waiting for the problem to grow wastes the chance to fix it cheaply.
std
II.A.2
A team is mapping an order-entry process. Which item is a process step rather than an input or an output?
Customer purchase order received by email
Order acknowledgment sent to the customer
Verify the customer's credit limit
Current price list from the pricing database
A step is an activity that transforms inputs; verifying credit is work done inside the process. The purchase order and price list feed the process, and the acknowledgment is something it produces.
std
II.A.2
A team studying invoice errors keeps drifting into purchasing and shipping problems. What should it have set at the start to prevent this?
The control limits for the weekly invoice error rate
The ground rules for how team meetings will be run
Where the process starts and where it ends
The sigma level the billing process is expected to reach
Clear start and stop points keep the team inside the process it was chartered to fix. Ground rules govern behavior in meetings, not what the project covers.
std
II.A.2
Order-to-ship time is 30 days, yet sales, engineering and production each meet their own departmental targets. What is the most likely explanation?
Delays build up at the handoffs between departments, which no one owns
The departmental targets were set too loosely by each manager
Production is the bottleneck and is hiding its true cycle time
Customers are changing their orders more often than they did

When each function optimizes its own piece, the waits and errors at the handoffs between them are nobody's job. Loose targets might matter, but they would not explain why every department looks fine while the whole process is slow.
std
II.A.2
A project must improve a claims process that runs through four departments. Which step does the most to overcome the cross-functional challenge?
Name an end-to-end process owner with authority across the departments involved
Ask each department head to improve their own portion of the process
Limit the project scope to the department with the most defects
Have each department report its own cycle time to the team weekly

Cross-functional processes need someone accountable for the whole flow, or each department keeps optimizing its own part. Splitting the work by department repeats the same suboptimization that created the problem.
std
II.A.2
A process map starts at "order keyed" and ends at "order shipped". The sponsor's complaint is long waits before an order is keyed. What does this show?
The upstream boundary is set too late to include the problem
The map has too many steps to be useful to the team
The downstream boundary should be moved out to payment received
The process has no measurable output for the project
Boundaries must enclose the part of the process where the problem occurs; here the waiting happens before the chosen start point. Extending the end point does nothing for a delay at the front.
std
II.A.3
A firm compares its on-time delivery rate with figures published by its two main rivals. This is:
Collaborative benchmarking
Internal benchmarking
Competitive benchmarking
Best-practice benchmarking
Measuring yourself against direct competitors is competitive benchmarking. It is not collaborative, because the rivals are not partners sharing information.
std
II.A.3
Six hospitals agree to share infection-rate data and visit each other's wards to learn what works. This is:
Competitive benchmarking
Reverse engineering
Internal benchmarking
Collaborative benchmarking
Collaborative benchmarking is a group of organizations openly sharing data and practices for mutual learning. Competitive benchmarking compares against rivals, usually without their cooperation.
std
II.A.3
A parts distributor studies how a mail-order clothing retailer picks orders, because that retailer is known for very fast, accurate picking. This is:
Best-practice benchmarking
Competitive benchmarking
Collaborative benchmarking
Product benchmarking
Best-practice benchmarking looks for the best way to perform a process, often outside one's own industry. The retailer is not a competitor, so this is not competitive benchmarking.
std
II.A.3
What is the main practical limitation of competitive benchmarking?
It applies only to products and never to services
It requires a formal agreement among all industry members
Its results cannot be expressed as numerical measures
Rivals rarely share the methods behind their results

Competitors guard their methods, so competitive benchmarking often yields performance figures without the practices behind them. A formal agreement among members describes collaborative benchmarking, not a limit of competitive benchmarking.
std
II.A.3
A team adopts a benchmark partner's 2% scrap target but makes no other changes. What did the team miss?
Learning the practices behind the partner's results
Checking that the target is lower than the industry average
Choosing a partner from inside its own industry
Setting the target higher than the partner to look better

Benchmarking is valuable for the practices behind the numbers; a borrowed target without the methods changes nothing. Partner industry matters less, since best-practice benchmarking often looks outside one's own sector.
std
II.A.4
A team at the start of a project needs a one-page, high-level view of who supplies the process, what goes in, the main steps, what comes out and who receives it. Which tool fits?
Detailed swim-lane flowchart
Cause-and-effect diagram
Value stream map with timelines
SIPOC diagram
A SIPOC gives exactly this high-level view and helps set scope early in Define. A swim-lane flowchart goes to step-level detail that is not needed yet.
std
II.A.4
In a SIPOC diagram, the Process column normally contains:
About four to seven high-level steps
Every task, decision point and rework loop
The measures used to judge each output
The suspected root causes of the defects
SIPOC is a high-level map, so the process is shown in a handful of major steps. Every task and decision belongs in a detailed process map later.
std
II.A.4
On an injection molding process, which is a controllable input variable (X)?
Part weight after ejection
Mold temperature setpoint
Flash on the part edge
Critical bore diameter
Inputs are the factors that drive the result, and mold temperature can be set by the operator. Part weight, flash and bore size are outputs (Ys) the process produces.
std
II.A.4
Ambient humidity changes coating thickness, but operators cannot set it. In the input-output analysis it is best classed as:
A controllable input
A process output
A customer requirement
A noise input
Noise inputs affect the output but are not controlled in normal operation. Calling it controllable would imply operators can set it, which they cannot.
std
II.A.4
A team suspects hold pressure drives part thickness. What is the best first way to evaluate the relationship?
Plot paired readings of thickness and hold pressure on a scatter diagram
Build a Pareto chart of thickness defects broken out by shift and machine
Draw a histogram of part thickness and compare its spread with the tolerance
Add hold pressure to the Inputs column of the SIPOC and move on to Analyze
Evaluating an input-output relationship needs paired X and Y data, and a scatter diagram shows it directly. A histogram of thickness alone shows the spread of Y but says nothing about what drives it.
std
II.A.4
A green belt writes Y = f(X1, X2, X3) for a curing process. What does this express?
The output is the average of the three listed inputs
The three inputs are independent of each other
The output depends on the listed inputs
The output must be controlled before the inputs are measured
Y = f(X) states that output performance is a function of input variables, a relationship the team then tests with data. It says nothing about averaging or about whether the inputs are independent.
std
II.A.5
A team is improving a returns process. Who should be accountable for keeping the gains after the team disbands?
The process owner
The green belt who led the work
The finance analyst who validated savings
The facilitator of the team meetings
The process owner manages the process day to day and has authority over it, so long-term control belongs there. The green belt moves on to other work once the project closes.
std
II.A.5
A team plans to change when the test lab picks up samples. Besides lab staff, who should be identified as stakeholders?
Only the lab manager, since the lab owns the pickup schedule
The corporate finance office, since all changes affect cost
No one else, since the change is internal to the lab
Groups that depend on the schedule, such as production
Stakeholders include anyone affected by or able to affect the change; production and shipping wait on lab results. Treating it as purely a lab matter is how downstream groups get surprised.
std
II.A.5
A stakeholder analysis shows the warehouse manager has high influence and is strongly opposed to the project. What should the green belt do?
Leave the manager off the distribution list until the results are final
Meet the manager early to understand the concerns and involve him in the plan
Ask the sponsor to order the manager to support the project
Narrow the scope so that the warehouse is no longer affected

Influential, resistant stakeholders need early engagement so their concerns can be heard and addressed. Bypassing or overruling him tends to harden resistance at the moment his support will be needed.
std
II.A.5
A project will change how a process runs. Who usually has the authority to approve those changes?
The process owner, who has authority over it
The newest team member, who has the freshest view
The customer, who receives the process output
The supplier, who provides the main process input
Process owners hold the authority and accountability for a process, so they approve changes and must be identified early. Customers and suppliers are stakeholders but do not control the process.
std
II.B.1
Which group is an internal customer of a machining department?
The steel mill that supplies its bar stock
The distributor that buys the finished product
The bank that finances the new machines
The assembly department that uses its parts
An internal customer is the next process inside the organization that receives the work. The distributor is an external customer, and the mill is a supplier.
std
II.B.1
A firm makes brake pads that are sold through parts distributors to repair shops, which fit them to customers' cars. Which list best identifies its external customers?
Only the distributors, because they pay the invoices
The sales and purchasing departments
The raw-material and packaging suppliers
Distributors, repair shops and vehicle owners
External customers include everyone outside the firm who receives or uses the product along the chain, not only the party that pays. Sales and purchasing are internal functions.
std
II.B.1
A team plans to switch to a cheaper carton to cut packaging cost. What should it do before the change is approved?
Confirm that the new carton costs less than the old carton does
Ask the carton supplier to certify that the new design is sound
See how the new carton affects internal and external customers
Change the carton first and then track any complaints afterward
Identifying customers includes judging what the project will do to them, such as damage in transit for buyers or handling problems for the warehouse. Cost alone ignores those effects.
std
II.B.1
A billing team cuts its cycle time by skipping a data check. Within weeks, collections staff spend more time fixing disputes. What does this show?
The external customer was the only one that mattered
Collections should have been made part of billing
It overlooked an internal customer it affected
Cycle time was the wrong measure for billing to use
Collections receives billing's output and is an internal customer; the change shifted work onto it. Identifying all affected customers up front would have exposed this effect.
std
II.B.2
A company wants to measure satisfaction across 4,000 customers at low cost and compare results by region. Which method fits best?
A series of focus groups
One-on-one interviews
A structured survey
Direct observation of use
Surveys reach large numbers at low cost and give comparable data across groups. Focus groups give depth but cannot cover thousands of customers cheaply.
std
II.B.2
A team wants to explore how customers react to a new service concept and to hear them build on each other's ideas. Which method fits best?
A mailed survey
A warranty data review
A focus group
A mystery shopper visit
Focus groups use guided group discussion, so participants react to and build on each other's comments. A mailed survey collects answers in isolation.
std
II.B.2
A sales manager needs in-depth detail from five key accounts about why orders were lost, including topics they may not discuss in front of others. Which method fits best?
A focus group of all five accounts
A short online survey
A review of complaint logs
Individual interviews
One-on-one interviews allow depth and privacy for sensitive topics. Putting competing accounts in one focus group would discourage frank answers.
std
II.B.2
Users of a hand tool say they are satisfied, yet returns for wrist strain keep rising. Which method is most likely to reveal the problem?
Sending a longer satisfaction survey with more rating scales
Watching users work with the tool in their normal setting
Holding a focus group to ask what features they would like
Reviewing the tool's design drawings against the specification
Observation captures what customers actually do, including needs they do not voice. Another survey asks the same people who already said they were satisfied.
std
II.B.2
What is the main flaw in the survey question "How much do you like our improved, faster delivery service?"
It asks about two different services at the same time
It leads respondents toward a favorable answer
It uses a rating scale that is too wide
It gives respondents too many answer choices
Words such as "improved" and "faster" signal the answer the company wants, which biases results. It does not combine two services, so it is not double-barreled.
std
II.B.2
A survey asks, "Was the technician prompt and courteous?" with yes or no answers. What is the problem?
It leads respondents toward a favorable answer
It asks about two things in one question
It should use open-ended answers instead
It asks about something customers cannot judge
A double-barreled question mixes two attributes; a "no" could mean late, rude or both. Splitting it into two questions fixes this.
std
II.B.2
A survey asks, "Do you use our product regularly?" What is the best way to improve it?
Replace "regularly" with set choices such as daily or weekly
Add "strongly agree" and "strongly disagree" as answer choices
Move the question to the end of the survey form
Ask respondents to explain their answer in writing
"Regularly" means different things to different people, so answers are ambiguous; defined frequency choices remove the vagueness. Adding agreement choices does not fix what the word means.
std
II.B.2
Before sending a survey to all customers, what is the best way to catch confusing or biased questions?
Have the marketing team approve the final wording
Increase the sample size to offset unclear questions
Pilot the survey with a small group from the target population
Add a comments box at the end of the survey form
A pilot test with real respondents exposes wording problems before full release. A bigger sample only repeats the same misunderstanding more times.
std
II.B.2
A customer survey has an 8% response rate. What is the main concern about the results?
Those who replied may not represent the rest
The questions were probably too easy to answer
The rating scale must have had too few points
The data cannot be summarized with percentages
Low response invites nonresponse bias: people who answer often hold stronger views than the rest. A representative response is a key element of an effective survey.
std
II.B.2
In a focus group, one participant answers every question first and others start agreeing with him. Which element of an effective focus group is missing?
A larger, quieter room so that participants feel at ease
A longer list of questions for the session
A skilled moderator who draws out every participant
A written survey handed out after the session
Focus groups depend on a moderator who keeps one voice from steering the group. More questions would give the dominant person more chances to talk.
std
II.B.3
In a QFD house of quality, what does the central relationship matrix show?
How strongly each technical characteristic affects each customer requirement
How the technical characteristics trade off against one another in the design
How the company's product compares with competitors' products
How much each customer requirement costs the company to meet
The central matrix links the customer's "whats" to the design "hows". Trade-offs among the technical characteristics appear in the roof, not the central matrix.
std
II.B.3
In a house of quality, the roof shows that raising motor power sharply reduces battery life. How should the team use this?
As proof that customers rate motor power above battery life
As a trade-off between technical characteristics that needs a decision
As a sign that one of the two requirements should be dropped from the product
As a competitor rating to show in the right-hand section
The roof is the correlation matrix among technical characteristics, flagging trade-offs to resolve. It does not show customer priority, which comes from importance ratings.
std
II.B.3
A CTQ tree starts with the need "fast service". Which item is the best CTQ at the end of a branch?
Customers feel valued when they call the service line
Phone calls answered within 30 seconds
The call center is well staffed
Agents are friendly and helpful
A CTQ must be specific and measurable so it can be checked against a target. The other items are still vague needs or drivers that need further breakdown.
std
II.B.3
In a CTX breakdown, the team tags each requirement with the area it most affects. A guard that keeps fingers out of a pinch point is tagged:
Critical to safety
Critical to delivery
Critical to cost
Critical to process
CTX lets the X be quality, cost, delivery, safety and so on; a finger guard exists to prevent injury. It has no main effect on delivery.
std
II.B.3
Why might a team use a CTX approach rather than listing only critical-to-quality characteristics?
CTX replaces the need to gather the voice of the customer
Cost, delivery and safety needs are captured with quality
CTX requires fewer customer requirements to be analyzed overall
CTX ranks the requirements without any customer input
CTX widens the view so that what is critical to cost, delivery or safety is translated into measures too. It still depends on voice-of-the-customer data, not instead of it.
std
II.B.3
Hotel guests never praise clean sheets, but they complain loudly when sheets are not clean. In the Kano model, clean sheets are:
A performance requirement
A basic (must-be) requirement
A delighter (attractive) feature
An indifferent feature
Basic requirements cause dissatisfaction when absent but no extra satisfaction when present. A performance requirement raises satisfaction steadily as it improves, which clean sheets do not.
std
II.B.3
For a car, customer satisfaction rises steadily as fuel economy improves. In the Kano model this is:
A basic (must-be) requirement
A performance requirement
A delighter feature
A reverse feature
Performance (one-dimensional) requirements give more satisfaction the better they are met. A delighter is something customers do not expect at all.
std
II.B.3
A feature that delighted customers five years ago is now taken for granted. What does the Kano model say about this?
The feature was never truly a delighter at all
Customers have stopped valuing the feature
Delighters tend to become expected over time
The feature should now be removed
Customer expectations move, so attractive features drift toward performance and then basic requirements. Removing it would now cause dissatisfaction, because customers expect it.
std
II.B.3

A team weights complaint mentions ×3, expedite requests ×2 and survey mentions ×1. Late delivery has 10 complaint mentions, packaging has 25 survey mentions, and lead time has 4 expedite requests. Which issue ranks highest after weighting?
Late delivery
Packaging
Lead time
Packaging and late delivery tie
Weighted scores are late delivery 10 × 3 = 30, packaging 25 × 1 = 25 and lead time 4 × 2 = 8. Packaging leads only on raw counts, before weighting.
std
II.B.3
Why would a team give a product complaint more weight than a routine survey response?
It signals real dissatisfaction and greater urgency
Complaints are easier to count than survey responses
Survey responses are always biased toward praise
Complaints come from the company's largest accounts
Weighting amplifies input that signals greater importance or urgency, and a complaint reflects a real failure the customer took action on. Ease of counting is not a reason to weight data.

0 days
2 days

6 days
8 days
9 days
7 days

Executive

The process owner

Each person must give exactly one idea
Only the leader may write ideas down
Judging ideas is held back until generation is over

Ideas are ranked at the same time they are given
Everyone gets a turn, so quieter members contribute

A team includes a forceful manager, and newer members hesitate to speak. Which technique best gives everyone equal say in generating and ranking options?
Open free-for-all discussion
Nominal group technique
Decision by the manager
A show of hands on each idea

In nominal group technique, five members rank four ideas (4 = best). Idea W totals 17, X 12, Y 13 and Z 8. What should the team do?

Treat X as the team's top choice
Rank again until everyone gives W a 4
Drop the ranking and decide by discussion

A team has a list of 30 possible causes and needs to cut it to a few for further study. Which technique fits best?
Brainstorming
Multivoting
A force-field analysis
A Gantt chart

In multivoting, how are votes usually used?
Each person gets one vote, and the top item is chosen at once
Only the leader votes, after hearing each member's view
Each person gets several votes, and items are cut in rounds
Votes are weighted by each member's job title

A shared action log and brief stand-up
A monthly report sent to the sponsor
An annual review of the project's status
A poster at the plant entrance

II.F.4
The sponsor wants a brief status, while the operators affected want to know how their jobs will change. What should the green belt do?
Send both groups the same detailed technical report
Tailor the content and format to each audience
Brief only the sponsor and let operators hear later
Wait to tell anyone until the project is complete

II.F.4
A green belt is preparing for a phase review with the sponsor. What best supports a good review?
Every raw data file collected so far
A long list of all ideas the team discussed
A summary of results and decisions needed
A verbal update with no supporting material

II.F.4
A team wants to make sure each stakeholder group gets the right updates at the right time. Which tool fits best?
A RACI chart listing who does each task
A Gantt chart showing the task schedule
A communication plan
A fishbone diagram of communication problems

III.A
A loan application passes through intake, underwriting, compliance and funding, and most of the delay seems to occur between departments. Which map best shows where the handoffs and waits occur?
A SIPOC diagram listing the suppliers, inputs and outputs of the process
A spaghetti diagram tracing how the paper file moves around the office
A detailed flowchart of the underwriting steps alone
A cross-functional (swim-lane) map with one lane per department
A swim-lane map puts each department in its own lane, so every handoff and queue between groups is visible. A SIPOC is deliberately high level and does not show handoffs or waits step by step.

III.A
A team draws its as-is process map in a conference room, working from the current written procedure. What is the main weakness of this approach?
It produces a map with more detail than the team needs
It leaves out the customer requirements for the process
It makes the map impossible to compare with the procedure
It shows how the process should run, not how it runs

An as-is map must be built by walking the process with the people who do the work; copying the procedure produces a should-be map and hides the very gaps the team is looking for. Missing customer requirements is a SIPOC concern, not the core flaw here.

III.A
While walking a process, a team sees operators routinely skip a documented inspection step because a new fixture makes the defect impossible. What should the team do first?
Retrain the operators to follow every step of the procedure exactly as written
Rewrite the procedure on the spot so that it matches what operators now do
Leave the procedure and the practice alone because the parts are good
Log the gap for the procedure owner to resolve

A mismatch between procedure and practice is a gap to be resolved by the document owner, who confirms the right method and then aligns the document and the practice. Retraining first assumes the document is right; rewriting on the spot skips the review that confirms the fixture really removes the risk.

III.A

Reviewing work instructions at a packaging line, a Green Belt finds one that tells operators to set sealing temperature on a controller model the line replaced last year. What does this finding indicate?
The operators are not following the work instruction as they should
The packaging line has a training gap but no documentation gap
The process map for the line must have been drawn incorrectly
The work instruction is misaligned with the process and needs revision

An instruction that refers to equipment no longer in use no longer matches the process; it is a documentation gap that must be corrected through document control. Nothing in the finding shows operators are at fault, since they cannot follow steps for equipment that is gone.

III.A
When mapping a process, a team reaches a step where an inspector either sends a part to rework or passes it forward based on a visual check. How should this appear on the flowchart?
As a single process box labeled visual check
As a document symbol for the inspection record
As a delay symbol before the next process step
As a decision symbol with two labeled exit paths

A step with alternative outcomes is a decision and is drawn as a diamond with each exit labeled (for example pass and fail). A plain process box hides the rework loop, which is often where the waste is.

III.A
Comparing its as-is map with the documented process, a team finds a rework loop that appears in no procedure and that operators call normal. How should the team treat this loop?
As a hidden factory that should be measured and investigated
As an informal step that should be added to the procedure
As outside the scope because the procedure does not cover it
As normal variation that does not need any further study

Undocumented rework is a classic hidden factory: it consumes capacity and hides defects, so it is a gap to measure and attack. Writing it into the procedure would make waste official rather than remove it.

III.A
Two controlled procedures for final inspection of the same product give different acceptance limits for surface finish. What should the Green Belt do?
Use the tighter of the two limits for the project data and leave the documents as they are
Use the limit from whichever procedure was revised most recently and move on
Ask the inspectors which limit they prefer and record that as the requirement
Have the owners set one controlling limit and align both documents

Conflicting documents are a misalignment that the document owners must resolve against the real requirement, after which both documents are corrected. Picking a limit yourself, by date or by preference, leaves the conflict in place for everyone else.

Two independent inspections are made on each part. Probability of passing the first is 0.90 and of passing the second is 0.80. What is the probability that a part passes both?
For independent events P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.90 × 0.80 = 0.72. 0.98 is the chance of passing at least one, 1 − (0.10 × 0.20).

III.B.1
Each defect found is classified as exactly one of critical, major or minor. P(critical) = 0.02 and P(major) = 0.10. What is the probability that a defect is critical or major?
Because the classes are mutually exclusive, the probabilities simply add: 0.02 + 0.10 = 0.12. 0.118 wrongly subtracts an overlap of 0.002, which cannot exist when a defect can have only one class.

Events A and B are mutually exclusive, and each has a probability greater than zero. Which statement is true?
They cannot be independent, because if A occurs B cannot
They must be independent, because they never occur together
They are independent only if their probabilities are equal
They are independent if their probabilities add to one
If A occurs, P(B) drops to zero, so knowing A changes the probability of B; that is the opposite of independence. Never occurring together is what mutually exclusive means, not independent.

III.B.1
A tray holds 10 parts, 3 of them defective. Two parts are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both are defective?
Use the general multiplication rule: (3/10) × (2/9) = 6/90 = 0.067. 0.090 assumes replacement (0.3 × 0.3), which ignores that the first draw changes what is left.

III.B.1
At a distribution center 40% of orders are rush orders, and 5% of rush orders ship late. What is the probability that a randomly chosen order is a rush order that ships late?
P(rush and late) = P(rush) × P(late | rush) = 0.40 × 0.05 = 0.02. 0.05 is only the conditional probability of late given rush, not the joint probability.
std
III.B.1
Three of five available tests must be run in sequence, and the order affects the result. How many different test sequences are possible?
