std
III.B.1
A Green Belt needs 3 operators from a pool of 8 for a gauge study, and their order does not matter. How many different groups are possible?
Order does not matter, so use combinations: 8!/(3! × 5!) = 56. 336 is the permutation count, which counts each group six times over.

III.B.1
In which situation should permutations rather than combinations be used?
Choosing three of seven suppliers to audit in the coming quarter
Selecting three parts from a lot of seven to send for testing
Picking three of seven shifts to include in a capability study
Assigning leader, scribe and timekeeper among seven members

Distinct roles make order matter, since swapping who is leader and who is scribe gives a different assignment, so permutations apply. In the other cases only which items are chosen matters, which is a combination.

Which statement best describes the central limit theorem?
Sample means approach a normal distribution as n grows, whatever the population shape
Individual values tend toward a normal distribution once enough of them have been collected
The mean of any large sample will equal the population mean exactly
Sample standard deviations follow a normal distribution centered on zero

The theorem concerns the distribution of sample averages: with larger n it approaches normal with standard deviation σ/√n, even if individual values are not normal. Collecting more individual values does not change the shape of the population.

III.B.2
Individual cycle times have a standard deviation of 12 minutes. What is the standard deviation of averages of 9 cycle times?
1.3 minutes
4.0 minutes
12.0 minutes
36.0 minutes
The standard error of the mean is σ/√n = 12/√9 = 4. Dividing by n instead of √n gives 1.3.

III.B.2
Individual call handling times are strongly right-skewed. A team takes a random sample of 60 calls and builds a confidence interval for the mean. Why is a normal-based interval reasonable here?
The skew disappears once the times are sorted from low to high
A sample of 60 calls makes the individual times normally distributed
With n = 60 the distribution of the sample mean is close to normal
Confidence intervals do not depend on any distribution at all
The central limit theorem makes the sampling distribution of the mean nearly normal at moderate n, which is what the interval relies on. The individual times stay skewed however many are collected.

III.B.2
With σ known, a team wants to cut the width of a confidence interval for the mean in half. By what factor must the sample size change?
Multiply it by 2
Multiply it by √2
Multiply it by 8
Multiply it by 4
Interval width is proportional to σ/√n, so halving it needs √n to double, which means n multiplied by 4. Doubling n only shrinks the width by a factor of √2.

III.B.2
A team uses a test on the mean of 50 shipping weights, though individual weights are not normal. What makes the test's p-value trustworthy?
The mean of 50 values has a near-normal sampling distribution
The p-value is unaffected by the shape of any distribution
Testing the mean removes the need for a random sample
Fifty weights are enough to make the weights themselves normal

III.B.2
Individual diameters from a turning process are somewhat skewed. Why is an X-bar chart with subgroups of 5 less affected by this than a chart of individual values?
Subgroups of five remove the skew from each individual reading
Subgroup averages are closer to normal than the individual values
X-bar charts use the specification limits instead of the data
X-bar charts are not built on any assumption about variation

Poisson
Chi-square
Binomial
F

A team counts paint blemishes on each car door. Each door has many places a blemish could occur, but blemishes are rare at any one spot. Which distribution best models the count per door?
Binomial
Normal
Student's t
Poisson

A team wants to know whether a filling process's standard deviation now differs from its long-standing value of 1.5 g. Which distribution does the test use?
Chi-square
Student's t
F
Poisson

III.C
Which statement correctly describes the chi-square distribution?
It is symmetric about zero and has heavier tails than the normal at small sample sizes
It is nonnegative and right-skewed, with shape set by its degrees of freedom
It is the ratio of two sample variances and has two degrees-of-freedom values
It describes counts of defects per unit when defects occur at a constant rate

III.C
Compared with the standard normal distribution, Student's t distribution:
Has lighter tails and moves away from the normal as degrees of freedom rise
Is skewed right and is used for comparing two variances
Has heavier tails and approaches the normal as degrees of freedom rise
Is discrete and used for counts of defective units

III.C
A Green Belt has 8 measurements, σ unknown, and wants a confidence interval for the mean. Which distribution should she use?
Standard normal z
Chi-square with 7 degrees of freedom
F with 7 and 8 degrees of freedom
t with 7 degrees of freedom

std
III.C
Two molding machines make the same part. The team wants to test whether their variances differ. Which distribution is used?
F
Chi-square
Student's t
Binomial
The ratio of two sample variances follows the F distribution, which is the basis of the two-variance test (and of ANOVA). Chi-square tests one variance against a known value.

Which of these is continuous (variables) data?
Number of scratches on each panel
Fill weight of each bottle in grams
Pass or fail result for each bottle
Number of late shipments each week

A team stops recording shaft diameters and records only in spec or out of spec. What is the main consequence?
Attributes data become variables data, so the analysis becomes more sensitive
The data move from an ordinal scale to a ratio scale with a true zero
Variables data become attributes, so larger samples are needed

Defects are recorded by type: scratch, dent, stain and burr. What measurement scale is this?
Ordinal
Interval
Ratio
Nominal

III.D.1
Customers rate service on a 1 to 5 scale from very poor to excellent. A manager wants to report the average rating. What is the concern?

The scale is nominal, so the ratings have no meaningful order
The scale is ratio, so a geometric mean must be used
The scale is interval, so the median cannot be used

Celsius is an ordinal scale with unequal steps
Celsius is an interval scale with no true zero
Celsius is a nominal scale of named categories
Celsius is a ratio scale, so differences are invalid
On an interval scale differences are meaningful but ratios are not, because 0 °C is not an absence of heat. Ratios are valid only on a ratio scale such as kelvin.

III.D.1
Which of these is measured on a ratio scale?
Temperature in degrees Fahrenheit
Supplier ranking from first to fifth
Cycle time in seconds
Machine number on the shop floor

III.D.2
A Green Belt needs a simple random sample of 50 invoices from a file of 2,000. Which method gives one?
Take the 50 invoices that sit at the front of the file drawer
Take the 50 largest invoices because they carry the most risk
Take 50 invoices from the clerk who processes the most of them
Number every invoice and pick 50 with a random number generator

III.D.2
Defect rates are thought to differ among three shifts, and the team wants a precise estimate for each one. Which sampling approach fits best?

One simple random sample drawn from all of the output
A sample taken only from the shift with the worst results
Collecting whatever parts are easiest to reach at the end of the day

std
III.D.2
Lines 1, 2 and 3 produce 50%, 30% and 20% of output. A proportionally stratified sample of 200 parts should take how many from each line?
Proportional allocation applies each line's share to the total sample: 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2 times 200. Equal allocation (67, 67, 66) ignores the different volumes.
std
III.D.2
Operators need to record which defects occur on a molded housing and where on the part each one appears. Which tool fits best?
A run chart of the daily defect total for each operator
A scatter diagram of defect count against cycle time
A check sheet with a drawing of the part to mark defect locations
A free-text log where operators describe each defect
A location (concentration) check sheet captures both type and position quickly and consistently at the point of work. A free-text log is slow to fill in and hard to tally.
std
III.D.2
Readings near 12.0000 mm are coded as (x − 12.0000) × 10,000 so operators write short whole numbers. What coded value is recorded for 12.0047 mm?
(12.0047 − 12.0000) × 10,000 = 0.0047 × 10,000 = 47. Coding cuts recording errors, and the original value can be recovered by reversing the steps.
std
III.D.2
Data are coded by subtracting 12.0000 and multiplying by 10,000. The coded data have a standard deviation of 6. What is the standard deviation of the original data?
6 mm
Subtracting a constant does not change spread; multiplying scales it, so divide by 10,000: 6/10,000 = 0.0006 mm. Adding 12.0000 back applies only to the mean, not the standard deviation.
std
III.D.2
Two inspectors record surface defect counts on the same panels and get very different totals. What should the data collection plan have included?
A larger sample of panels from each of the two inspectors
A rule that all counts be entered into the system daily
A weekly chart comparing the counts from each inspector
A clear operational definition of a surface defect
When people count different things under the same name, the fix is a clear operational definition, ideally with boundary examples. More data collected with inconsistent definitions only adds noise.
std
III.D.2
Which set of items belongs in a data collection plan for a Measure phase?
Measures, methods, owners, timing, sample size and data checks
The root causes of the problem and the solutions the team will pilot
The project charter, team roster and stakeholder communication plan
The control limits and reaction plan for the improved process
A data collection plan defines the measures, their operational definitions, the method, responsibility, timing, sampling and data quality checks. Root causes and control plans come in later phases.
std
III.D.2
A file of 500 fill weights for a 500 g product shows a minimum of 0 g and a maximum of 512 g. What should the Green Belt do before analysis?
Keep them all, since every value came from the same system
Investigate the zero values as likely missing or erroneous entries
Delete the largest values, since they are farthest from target
Replace each zero with the average of all the other weights

A min/max check that finds an impossible value such as 0 g signals a recording error or a blank stored as zero; the cause must be found before the data are used. Quietly replacing values with the average hides the problem and distorts the spread.
std
III.D.2
A cycle-time column in an exported data set has 30 blank cells and one entry of 4.2 among values that otherwise run from 38 to 46. What is the best approach?
Enter zero in each blank cell so that every record can be used in the analysis
Leave the data exactly as exported, because changing data is never appropriate
Trace each cause, then fix, recover or exclude the records and document it
Drop the 4.2 entry and all the blanks without recording what was removed

Null and erroneous values (4.2 looks like a slipped decimal for 42) need a traced cause and a documented treatment. Zeros would drag the mean down, and silent deletion makes the analysis impossible to audit.
std
III.D.3
A sample of five lead times is 4, 6, 7, 7 and 11 days. What is the sample standard deviation?
2.28 days
2.55 days
6.50 days
7.00 days
The squared deviations from the mean of 7 sum to 26; 26/(5 − 1) = 6.5, and √6.5 = 2.55. Dividing by n gives 2.28, the population formula.
std
III.D.3
Most repair jobs take 1 to 2 hours, but a few take over 20 hours. Which measure best reports a typical repair time?
The mean
The range
The variance
The median
A few very long jobs pull the mean upward, while the median stays at the middle job. Range and variance measure spread, not a typical value.
std
III.D.3
A data set has a mean of 48 and a median of 41. What does this most likely indicate?
It is skewed to the right
It is skewed toward the left
It is symmetric about its center
It contains no outliers
When a long upper tail pulls the mean above the median, the data are right-skewed. Left skew would put the mean below the median.
std
III.D.3
Why is the standard deviation usually preferred to the range for describing spread in a sample of 30?
It is always smaller and so easier to meet
It uses every value instead of only the two extremes
It is quicker to calculate by hand on the floor
It is in squared units, so it weights big values
The standard deviation draws on all 30 values and is less driven by one unusual point. The range uses only the largest and smallest values, so it wastes information as n grows.
std
III.D.3
Line A makes 200 g packs with s = 4 g. Line B makes 20 g packs with s = 1 g. Which statement is correct?
Line A is more variable, because its standard deviation is four times larger
The lines are equally variable once the packs are converted to kilograms
Line B is more variable relative to its mean, as its CV is higher
The variability cannot be compared because the two products are different
The coefficient of variation (s/mean) compares spread relative to size: 4/200 = 2% and 1/20 = 5%. Comparing raw standard deviations ignores the tenfold difference in mean.
std
III.D.3
Forty parts are grouped by diameter (mm): 9.8 to under 9.9: 4; 9.9 to under 10.0: 10; 10.0 to under 10.1: 18; 10.1 to under 10.2: 6; 10.2 to under 10.3: 2. Which class contains the median?
9.9 to under 10.0
10.1 to under 10.2
9.8 to under 9.9
10.0 to under 10.1
The median lies between the 20th and 21st values. Counting up, 4 + 10 = 14 values lie below 10.0 and 32 below 10.1, so it falls in the 10.0 class. The 9.9 class holds only values 5 through 14.
std
III.D.3
Using the same 40 diameters (classes 9.8, 9.9, 10.0, 10.1, 10.2 with counts 4, 10, 18, 6, 2), what percentage of parts measure under 10.1 mm?
The cumulative frequency up to 10.1 is 4 + 10 + 18 = 32, and 32/40 = 80%. 45% is the share of the 10.0 class alone, not the cumulative share.
std
III.D.3
A set of delivery times contains a few extreme values that have been confirmed as real. Which pair of measures best summarizes center and spread?
Median and IQR
Mean and standard deviation
Mode and the range
Mean and the range
The median and interquartile range resist the pull of extreme values, so they describe the bulk of the data well. The mean and standard deviation are both strongly affected by a few extreme values.
std
III.D.4
A team wants to see whether oven temperature is related to coating thickness, using 40 paired readings. Which graph should it build?
Histogram
Scatter diagram
Stem-and-leaf plot
Pareto chart
A scatter diagram plots one variable against the other and shows the form and strength of any relationship. A histogram shows the distribution of a single variable.
std
III.D.4
A scatter diagram of training hours against error rate shows a clear downward pattern. What is the most accurate conclusion?
Training causes fewer errors, so the training hours should be increased for all staff
There is no relationship, because the points do not fall exactly on a line
They are associated, but the plot alone does not prove cause
Error rate drives training hours, since the pattern runs downward
A scatter diagram shows association; a lurking variable such as experience could drive both. Proving cause needs a controlled study or strong process knowledge.
std
III.D.4
On a normal probability plot, 50% of values fall at 20.0 and 84% fall at 22.5. If the points lie on a straight line, what is the estimated standard deviation?

On a normal plot the 50th percentile estimates the mean, and the 84th percentile is about one standard deviation above it, so σ ≈ 22.5 − 20.0 = 2.5. Treating the gap as two standard deviations gives 1.25.
std
III.D.4
On a normal probability plot of tensile strength, the points bend steadily away from the straight line in a curve. What does this suggest?
The data are normal, because every point appears on the plot
The measurement system has too little resolution for the data
The sample is too large for a normal probability plot to work
The data probably are not normal
Normal data fall close to a straight line on this plot; a systematic curve indicates skew or another non-normal shape. Points simply appearing on the plot says nothing about the fit.
std
III.D.4
A histogram of bore diameters from a multi-cavity molding process shows two distinct peaks. What is the most likely explanation?
Two different process streams have been mixed in one data set
The process is normal and well centered between the limits
Too few classes were used to build the histogram
The gauge used has a bias that is larger than its tolerance

A bimodal histogram usually means a mixture of two process streams with different means, such as two cavities, machines or lots; stratifying the data by source will confirm it. Too few classes would tend to hide peaks, not create two clear ones.
std
III.D.4
A histogram of supplier inspection data rises steeply and then stops sharply at the upper specification, with no values beyond it. What does this most likely indicate?
The supplier's process is very capable at that end
Parts above the limit were screened out or the data were edited
The class width chosen for the histogram is too large
The process mean sits exactly at the upper specification
Natural processes taper off gradually; a sharp cutoff at a specification limit points to sorting or data censoring before reporting. A capable process would show a tail ending well inside the limit.
std
III.D.4
A stem-and-leaf plot (stem = tens, leaf = units) reads: 3 | 1 4 8; 4 | 0 2 2 5 9; 5 | 3 6. What is the median?
The ten values are 31, 34, 38, 40, 42, 42, 45, 49, 53, 56; the 5th and 6th are both 42, so the median is 42. 43 is the mean, not the median.
std
III.D.4
What does a stem-and-leaf plot offer that a histogram of the same data does not?
It shows the relationship between two variables
It tests whether the data come from a normal distribution
It keeps each individual data value visible
It shows the data in the order they were collected
A stem-and-leaf plot shows the shape of the distribution like a histogram while retaining the actual values. It shows neither time order nor relationships between two variables.
std
III.D.4
A box plot of cure times has Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 28 minutes. Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, above what value would a point be flagged as an outlier?
32 minutes
36 minutes
40 minutes
52 minutes
IQR = 28 − 20 = 8, and the upper fence is Q3 + 1.5 × 8 = 40. 36 uses 1 × IQR instead of 1.5.
std
III.D.4
A team wants to compare the center, spread and outliers of fill volumes from five filling heads in one graph. Which display fits best?
A single histogram of all the volumes
A scatter diagram of volume against time
One stem-and-leaf plot of all the data
Side-by-side box plots, one per head
Box plots placed side by side make it easy to compare medians, interquartile ranges and outliers across groups. A single combined histogram would blend the heads together and hide the differences.
std
III.E
In a gauge R&R study, one appraiser measures the same part several times with the same gauge and gets different readings. This variation is called:
Repeatability
Reproducibility
Linearity
Stability
Repeatability (equipment variation) is the spread of repeated readings by one appraiser on one part with one gauge. Reproducibility is the difference between appraisers.
std
III.E
A gauge study gives σ(repeatability) = 0.03 and σ(reproducibility) = 0.04. Total observed σ is 0.125. What is %GRR of total variation, and how is it usually judged?
56%, generally unacceptable
40%, generally unacceptable
16%, conditionally acceptable
40%, conditionally acceptable

Standard deviations combine by root sum of squares: σ(GRR) = √(0.03² + 0.04²) = 0.05, and 0.05/0.125 = 40%, above the common 30% ceiling. Adding the standard deviations directly gives 56%; the variance ratio gives 16%.
std
III.E
A gauge R&R shows repeatability is large while reproducibility is very small. Where should the improvement effort go first?
Appraiser training, since appraisers disagree
The parts used, since they vary too little
The gauge and its fixturing
The tolerance, since it is too tight to meet
Large repeatability points to the instrument: wear, poor clamping, resolution or method. Appraiser training targets reproducibility, which is already small here.
std
III.E
When setting up a gauge R&R study, which practice is correct?
Choose parts close to nominal so that the readings are consistent for every appraiser
Have each appraiser measure all repeats of one part back to back before moving on
Let appraisers see their earlier readings so they can confirm their own results
Span the process range; measure in random, blind order
Parts must represent real process variation, and randomized blind measurement stops appraisers from remembering or adjusting readings. Parts all near nominal shrink part variation and inflate %GRR.
std
III.E
A supplier's CMM and the customer's CMM each measure the same 20 parts. The correlation is r = 0.98, but every customer reading is about 0.02 mm higher. What is the best conclusion?
They rank parts alike but have a systematic offset
The systems agree, since a correlation of 0.98 shows that they match
The systems disagree at random, so neither can be used to accept parts
The parts must have changed between the two measurement visits

High correlation shows the two systems move together, but it cannot reveal a constant offset; the 0.02 mm bias between them must be found and corrected. A random disagreement would not produce such a high correlation.
std
III.E
A reference standard of 25.000 mm is measured 10 times. The readings average 25.012 mm. What is the gauge bias?
−0.012 mm, so the gauge reads low
+0.012 mm, so the gauge reads high
+0.012 mm, so the gauge reads low
Not known without a full gauge R&R study
Bias = observed average − reference value = 25.012 − 25.000 = +0.012 mm, meaning readings run high. A GR&R measures precision and is not needed to estimate bias.
std
III.E
A gauge shows bias of −0.002 mm at the low end of its range and +0.010 mm at the high end. What does this describe?
Repeatability, as repeat readings vary
Stability, as bias changes over time
Linearity, as bias varies across the range
Reproducibility, as appraisers disagree
Linearity is the change in bias across the operating range of the gauge. Stability would require readings of the same standard taken over time, which this study did not do.
std
III.E

In an attribute agreement study, an inspector judged 50 parts twice. She matched herself on 47 parts and matched the reference standard on both trials for 44 parts. What is her percent agreement with the standard?
Agreement with the standard is 44/50 = 88%. 94% (47/50) is her agreement with herself, which can be high even when she is consistently wrong.
std
III.E
A gauge has σ(GRR) = 0.005 mm. The part tolerance is 10.00 ± 0.10 mm. Using 6σ, what is the P/T ratio?
P/T = 6σ(GRR)/(USL − LSL) = 0.030/0.20 = 15%. Using 5.15σ instead of 6σ gives about 13%, and dividing σ alone by the tolerance gives 2.5%.
std
III.E
A gauge used to accept parts at final inspection shows P/T = 8%, but %GRR of total process variation is 45%. Which conclusion is best?
It is unacceptable for any use and should be replaced before the next production run
It is fully acceptable for every purpose, since P/T is the only ratio that matters
It needs a linearity study before either of the two ratios can be interpreted
Fit for accept/reject use but too coarse for tracking part-to-part variation

P/T compares measurement error with the tolerance, so it judges conformance decisions; %GRR compares it with process spread, so it judges SPC and improvement work. Here the process is much tighter than the tolerance, so the two answers differ.
std
III.F.1
Which statement correctly distinguishes natural process limits from specification limits?
Natural limits come from the data; specification limits from the customer
Natural limits are set by engineering; specification limits are calculated from process data
Natural limits and specification limits are equal once a process is in control
Natural limits are always tighter than the specification limits for any product

Natural process limits (mean ± 3σ of individuals) are the voice of the process; specification limits are the voice of the customer. Nothing forces them to line up, which is why capability must be checked.
std
III.F.1
A process is stable with mean 50.0 and σ = 0.4, and the specification is 49.0 to 51.0. What are the natural process limits, and what follows?
49.0 to 51.0, so all output will fall inside the specification
48.8 to 51.2, so some output falls outside the specification
49.6 to 50.4, so all output will fall inside the specification
48.8 to 51.2, so the process is unstable and out of control

Natural limits are 50.0 ± 3 × 0.4 = 48.8 to 51.2, wider than the specification, so a small share (about 1.2%) is out of spec. Being stable is different from being capable; the process is in control but not capable.
std
III.F.1
An X-bar chart shows all points within control limits and no patterns, yet 4% of parts are out of specification. What should the team conclude?
The process is out of control, so the team should search for special causes in the data
The control limits are wrong and should be reset to match the specification limits
Stable but not capable; reduce common-cause variation or move the mean
The process is acceptable, because a stable process cannot produce defects

Stability means predictable, not good: a stable process can still produce out-of-spec parts if its natural limits exceed the specification. Replacing control limits with specification limits confuses the voice of the process with the voice of the customer.
std
III.F.1
A supervisor draws specification limits on an X-bar chart and is pleased that all averages are well inside them. What is wrong with this?
Specification limits should be drawn on the range chart rather than on the X-bar chart
The averages ought to be compared with the target rather than with the limits
Nothing is wrong, because in-spec averages mean the parts are in spec
Averages vary less than parts, so bad parts can hide behind good averages
Specification limits apply to individual parts, while averages have spread σ/√n; good averages can hide bad parts. That is why specifications are never drawn on an X-bar chart.
std
III.F.1
Inspection of 200 units, each with 5 defect opportunities, found 30 defects. What is the DPMO?
DPMO = defects/(units × opportunities) × 1,000,000 = 30/1,000 × 1,000,000 = 30,000. 150,000 is DPU (0.15) expressed per million units, ignoring opportunities.
std
III.F.1
A part passes through three steps with first-pass yields of 95%, 90% and 98%. What is the rolled throughput yield?
RTY is the product of the step yields: 0.95 × 0.90 × 0.98 = 0.838. 94.3% is the average yield, which overstates the chance of passing every step first time.
std
III.F.1
A process has 0.15 defects per unit, and defects follow a Poisson distribution. What is the expected first-pass yield?
With Poisson defects, Y = e^(−DPU) = e^(−0.15) = 0.861. 85% simply subtracts DPU from 1, which ignores that some units carry more than one defect.
std
III.F.2
A team computes Cpk = 1.6 from 30 pieces, but the control chart of the same data shows several points beyond the limits. What is the best conclusion?
The Cpk is not meaningful until the special causes are removed
The process is capable, since a Cpk of 1.6 easily meets 1.33
The process is capable only if the points beyond limits are deleted
The process needs a larger sample of 100 pieces, then Cpk is valid

Capability indices predict future output only for a stable process; with special causes present the next lot may look nothing like this one. Deleting the points without finding their causes hides the instability rather than fixing it.
std
III.F.2
Which characteristic should a capability study focus on first?
The characteristic that is the easiest to measure
A critical-to-quality characteristic tied to the customer
The characteristic with the most data already on file
Every dimension listed on the part drawing at once
Capability effort should go to the characteristics that matter to the customer or to function, the CTQs. Ease of measurement or data on hand says nothing about importance.
std
III.F.2
Before starting a capability study, a team finds that its gauge has a %GRR of 45%. What should it do?
Collect the data anyway and divide the result by the %GRR
Use a larger sample size to make up for the gauge error
Fix the measurement system first
Report Pp and Ppk instead of Cp and Cpk to account for it
Measurement error adds to the observed spread and can make a good process look incapable; the measurement system must be fit before the study. A larger sample does not remove measurement error.
std
III.F.2
How should data for an initial capability study usually be collected?
In one block of consecutive parts taken from a single run on one shift
From the parts that have already passed final inspection and been shipped
From the setup pieces made right after each tool change on the line
In rational subgroups spread over enough time to show normal variation
Subgroups spread over time (for example 20 to 25 subgroups) capture shifts, lots and operators, so the indices reflect real performance. Inspected parts have been screened, which truncates the data.
std
III.F.2
Flatness data have a natural floor at zero and are strongly skewed to the right. What should the analyst do before reporting capability?
Use a non-normal fit or a transformation
Use the normal-based formulas, which are robust to any degree of skew
Remove the largest values until the data look roughly normal
Report Cp only, because Cp does not depend on the data's shape
Normal-based indices misstate the tail and the ppm out of spec for strongly skewed data, so a non-normal fit or transformation is needed. Removing large values discards real data.
std
III.F.2
A characteristic has an upper specification limit only: runout of 0.05 mm maximum. Which index applies?
Cp, since it uses the full tolerance
Cpu (upper capability) only
Cpl (lower capability) only
Cp and Cpk, averaged together

With a one-sided specification there is no tolerance width, so Cp cannot be calculated; capability is judged by the distance from the mean to the USL. Cpl needs a lower limit, which does not exist here.
std
III.F.2
A dimension is specified as 10.0 +0.3/−0.1 mm. The process mean is 10.0 mm and σ = 0.03 mm. What is Cpk?
The limits are 9.9 and 10.3. Cpl = (10.0 − 9.9)/0.09 = 1.11 and Cpu = (10.3 − 10.0)/0.09 = 3.33; Cpk is the smaller, 1.11. 2.22 is Cp, which ignores where the mean sits.
std
III.F.3
Specification is 9.4 to 10.6, and within-subgroup σ = 0.15. What is Cp?
Cp = (USL − LSL)/6σ = 1.2/0.9 = 1.33. 2.67 would come from using 3σ instead of 6σ in the denominator.
std
III.F.3
Using the same process (spec 9.4 to 10.6, σ = 0.15), the mean is 10.1. What is Cpk?
Cpu = (10.6 − 10.1)/0.45 = 1.11 and Cpl = (10.1 − 9.4)/0.45 = 1.56; Cpk takes the smaller value. 1.33 is Cp, which ignores centering.
std
III.F.3
For a process, Cp = 1.8 and Cpk = 0.9. What does this tell the team?
The spread is too wide, but the process is well centered
The process is centered and fully capable as it runs
Spread is fine, but the mean is off center
The process is unstable and needs a new control chart
Cp reflects spread alone, while Cpk adds centering; Cpk well below Cp means centering is the main problem. Recentering would bring Cpk close to 1.8.
std
III.F.3
A process shows within-subgroup σ = 0.10 and overall σ = 0.14. Which statement is correct?
Cp will be lower than Pp, since it uses the larger estimate
Cp and Pp will be equal, since they share the same limits
Pp will be higher than Cp, since the process is long term
Pp will be lower than Cp, which shows shifts between subgroups

Cp uses within-subgroup variation and Pp uses the overall standard deviation; a larger overall σ means between-subgroup shifts are inflating long-term spread. The specification limits are the same, but the denominators differ.
std
III.F.3
Specification is 49 to 51. Overall s = 0.20 and the mean is 50.3. What is Ppk?
Ppu = (51 − 50.3)/0.6 = 1.17 and Ppl = (50.3 − 49)/0.6 = 2.17; Ppk takes the smaller value. 1.67 is Pp, which ignores the off-center mean.
std
III.F.3
A new process has 30 consecutive parts from its first run and no evidence yet of statistical control. Which indices should be reported?
Preliminary Pp and Ppk
Cp and Cpk, labeled as long-term capability
Cpm only, because the target is known
No index, since the parts are all in spec

Without demonstrated stability, the indices describe only the parts made, so they are reported as preliminary performance (Pp, Ppk). Cp and Cpk imply a stable process whose future output can be predicted.
std
III.F.3
When is Cpm more informative than Cpk?
When the specification is one-sided and there is no lower limit
When any departure from target causes loss, even within spec
When the data are attributes, such as counts of defective units
When the process is unstable and the special causes are unknown

Cpm includes the distance between the mean and the target in its denominator, so it penalizes off-target running in the spirit of the Taguchi loss function. It needs a target and a two-sided specification, and like the others it assumes stability.
std
III.F.3
Specification is 7 to 13 with target 10. The process mean is 10.5 and σ = 0.5. What is Cpm?
Cpm = (USL − LSL)/(6√(σ² + (μ − T)²)) = 6/(6√0.5) = 1.41. 2.00 is Cp, which ignores the 0.5 offset from target.
std
III.F.3
A centered process has Cp = 2.0. How many standard deviations lie between the mean and each specification limit?
Cp = 2 means the tolerance spans 12σ, so each limit is 6σ from a centered mean; this is the six sigma process. 3 is the distance for Cp = 1.
std
III.F.3
A process has Cpk = 1.33. What is the distance from the mean to the nearer specification limit, in standard deviations?
Cpk = Z(min)/3, so Z(min) = 3 × 1.33 = 4.0. 3.0 corresponds to Cpk = 1.0.
std
III.F.4
The familiar figure of 3.4 DPMO for a six sigma process relies on which convention?
The process is assumed to be perfectly centered at all times
Only the defects at one specification limit are counted
The mean is assumed to drift up to 1.5σ over the long term
The standard deviation is assumed to double over time
A centered 6σ process would give about 0.002 DPMO; 3.4 DPMO is the one-sided tail beyond 4.5σ, after allowing a 1.5σ shift. The convention assumes the mean moves, not that σ doubles.
std
III.F.4
A team has measurements from only one shift on one day. What should it assume about long-term performance?
It will match, since a process that is capable short term stays capable
It will be better, since operators improve as they gain more practice
It cannot be estimated in any way until a full year of data exists
It will be worse, as short-term data miss later shifts and drifts

Short-term data capture mainly within-subgroup common-cause variation; over time, lots, tooling, people and conditions add more. The convention is to treat short-term indices as optimistic and, where no long-term data exist, to allow for a shift.
std
III.F.4
Why do short-term capability figures usually look better than long-term figures for the same process?
Long-term data include between-lot and tool shifts that short-term data miss
Long-term data are collected with less accurate gauges than the short-term data
Short-term data come from a different process than the one running long term
Short-term data are always taken in larger samples, which reduces σ
Long-term variation adds between-subgroup sources to the within-subgroup variation seen short term, so long-term σ is larger. Sample size changes the precision of the estimate, not the true σ.
std
III.F.4
A process has a long-term DPMO of 6,210, equal to a one-sided tail beyond Z = 2.5. Using the 1.5σ shift convention, what sigma level is reported?
Short-term sigma level = Z(long-term) + 1.5 = 2.5 + 1.5 = 4.0. Reporting 2.5 gives the long-term Z without the conventional adjustment.
std
III.F.4
From the same process, short-term data give Z = 4.2 and long-term data give Z = 3.0. What is the observed sigma shift?
The shift is Z(short-term) − Z(long-term) = 4.2 − 3.0 = 1.2σ. 1.5σ is only the default convention; when both kinds of data exist, the actual shift should be used.
std
III.F.4
A Green Belt has only short-term data giving Z(ST) = 5.0 and needs to estimate long-term performance. What does the usual convention give for Z(LT)?
Without long-term data the convention subtracts 1.5σ from the short-term value: 5.0 − 1.5 = 3.5. Adding the shift (6.5) runs the conversion in the wrong direction.
std
IV.A.1

A team measures shaft diameter at both ends of each shaft, on five consecutive shafts, once every hour. The chart shows large differences between the two ends of the same shaft but little change between shafts or between hours. Which family of variation dominates?
Temporal variation from hour to hour
Lot-to-lot variation in the bar stock
Positional variation within each shaft
Cyclical variation between consecutive shafts

The biggest spread is between two locations on the same piece, which is positional (within-piece) variation, often taper from alignment or setup. Cyclical variation would show up as big differences between consecutive shafts, which the chart does not show.
std
IV.A.1
A Green Belt plans a multi-vari study on a four-cavity injection molding process. Which sampling plan fits the study best?
Measure one part ten times to estimate the repeatability of the gauge first
Several consecutive shots from all cavities, repeated across shifts
Take one part per hour from a single cavity and record the time it was molded
Draw a random sample of 30 parts from the finished goods bin at the end of the week

It proves which single input causes the change in output by changing that input on purpose

Measure more positions on each part so that within-part variation is better known
Conclude that the process is now stable and that no further study is needed

There is under a 0.1% chance that the relationship seen in the data is real

The slope has been shown to be zero, so humidity has no effect on thickness
Humidity explains 38% of the variation in coating thickness in the sample

The residuals of the model must be normally distributed to make any prediction

A strong linear relationship; the score tends to drop as tool age rises

A prediction interval, wider than the interval for the mean response
A confidence interval for the slope, which shows the expected change in strength

Raise α to 0.15 after the fact so that the result becomes statistically significant

Lack of power
Sampling bias

An alpha error
A false alarm
A type I error
A type II error

The p-value of the data decreases
The power of the test increases

Lower α from 0.05 to 0.01
Use a two-sided test even though only increases matter
Increase the sample size for each group

Compute the test statistic and compare it with the p-value

There is a 95% chance that the alternative hypothesis is true

The machine means have been shown to be exactly equal
There is not enough evidence that the machine means differ
The machine means differ at the 79% confidence level
There is a 21% chance that the machines differ in mean

Paired t-test on matched bore readings

F-test comparing the two variances

ANOVA is the only test that can compare averages from independent samples
Running many t-tests raises the overall chance of a false difference
Running many t-tests requires the data to be paired by part and by supplier

At least one line mean differs, and follow-up comparisons are needed to find which
The five lines have unequal variances, so the ANOVA result should be set aside
The line with the highest sample mean is the only one that differs from the rest
All five line means differ from each other, so each line needs its own action plan

Paired t-test on shift totals

Two-sample t-test
F-test for variances
Paired t-test

The difference is significant at 96% confidence
The difference is significant, since p is below 0.05
The difference is not significant at the chosen level
The α should be relaxed to 0.05 to fit the result

Chi-square test
One-sample z-test
Paired t-test
One-sample t-test

Supplier means are equal, since the interval is centered near zero
The difference is not significant, since the interval includes zero
Supplier means differ by 0.85 units, the midpoint of the interval
The difference is significant, since most of the interval is above zero

That every group's sample size is larger than thirty observations
That every group has exactly the same mean so the F-test is valid
That the response data are counts of defects rather than measurements
That the residuals are roughly normal, independent and similar in spread

Measure the current state with any data at hand, then set targets that fit the result
Start actions on known problems, then pick metrics later that show the improvement

The two states cannot be compared until they use the same defined metric
The current state must be converted to ppm by multiplying the percent by 10,000

Line 3 makes ongoing progress toward excellence in every area it runs

First-pass yield of at least 97% on line 3 by the end of the fourth quarter

Yield and on-time delivery
Customer survey score only
On-time delivery only

Pick the most likely causes and test them against data

The top event causes both input events to occur

Neither factor matters because the grand mean stays the same
Pressure has a large effect and speed has little

A strong interaction between feed rate and tool type

The best catalyst depends on which temperature is used
Neither factor affects the response in any meaningful way
Each factor can be optimized on its own from main effects
The plot must be wrong because lines should be parallel

B matters through its interaction with A despite a zero main effect
B's effect is 25 because that is the average at its high level
B cannot be judged because the design has too few replicates

Main effects plots always overstate the size of each factor's effect on output
Strong interactions make the response impossible to measure with any reliability
Each main effect averages over the other factor and can hide opposite trends

Make the change and measure wait times in the months after
Model arrivals and service times in a simulation first

Repeat the bench trials with more engineers present to observe

A proof of concept tests feasibility; a pilot runs the solution live at small scale
A proof of concept is required by ISO 9001; a pilot test is purely optional for teams
A proof of concept measures cost savings; a pilot test measures customer satisfaction

Build ahead to the weekly forecast for that item
Ask the supervisor which item to build next today

A counter display that shows how many screws have been driven

Separate internal from external setup work

Running trial strokes to check the first piece of the run

Add a larger buffer between each step so no operation ever starves
Place the steps side by side in a cell and move one part at a time
Group the machines by type in separate departments for efficiency

Quick changeovers allow small batches, cutting queue time

A one-time capital project led by engineering to retool a line
A formal audit of a process against a written specification
Ongoing small improvements made by the people doing the work
A statistical study of capability done before a product launch

A kaizen blitz
Daily kaizen
A design review
A DMAIC project

A complex defect with unknown causes that needs months of data
Operators' small daily ideas for improving their own stations
A culture change that has to spread across all company sites
A scoped cell problem a team can fix in one focused week

Enough team members from outside the work area involved
A longer event, running two weeks instead of five days
Follow-up to hold the new standard work after the event
A larger budget for new equipment during the event week

Kaizen requires statistical tools; a blitz uses no data or measurement
Kaizen is ongoing and incremental; a blitz is a short, intensive event
Kaizen is led by managers only; a blitz is run by operators working alone
Kaizen is for office work; a blitz applies only to production lines

To show customers proof that each part met its drawing tolerance

To catch process changes early so causes get fixed

Variation from stable chance causes stays within predictable limits

Agree, because each light bottle is a special cause that must be removed
Recalculate the control limits using the specification limits instead
Stop charting until the operators can hold every bottle inside the specification
Stop adjusting; change the system to cut common cause variation

Common cause; leave the process alone because the parts meet specification
Special cause; recalculate the limits using the data from the new lot
Special cause; investigate the new resin lot and remove the cause

Normal common cause variation, since no point is beyond a limit
A measurement error that should be corrected by recalibrating
A shift in the process mean that should be investigated
Control limits that were set too wide and should be narrowed

Investigate for a special cause, since the process has signaled a change
Scrap the shaft, since a point beyond a limit means nonconforming product
Move the control limit up, since the specification allows the larger size

They allow the use of a single chart that tracks both location and spread
They show a drift toward a limit before any part is actually rejected

Fill weight of each carton measured on a scale
Torque applied to each fastener by a nut runner
Number of misprinted labels found on each roll
Time each customer waits on hold before an answer

It contains exactly five consecutive parts from the same machine and shift
It holds as many parts as possible so the cost of each sample is kept low

A steady upward trend, because each cavity adds its own fixed offset to the subgroup average

Five consecutive parts taken at set times within each shift
One part from each shift, combined into a daily subgroup of three
Fifteen parts taken at random across the whole day as one subgroup
One part per hour, pooled into a subgroup at the end of each week

Once per day, since control limits are based on the daily averages
As rarely as possible, since fewer subgroups keep the control limits stable
Often enough to catch the kinds of change the process is known to undergo
Only when an operator suspects that a problem has developed in the process

VI.A.3
An X̄-s chart has n = 5, a grand mean of 50.0 and s̄ = 2.0. Using A3 = 1.427, what is the upper control limit for the X̄ chart?
UCL = X̿ + A3·s̄ = 50.0 + 1.427 × 2.0 = 52.85. The value 52.68 comes from 3s̄/√n, which skips the c4 bias correction built into A3, and 54.18 adds B4·s̄, the s chart factor.
std
VI.A.3
A chemical plant gets one viscosity result per batch, and batches finish about every eight hours. Which control chart fits best?
X̄-R chart with subgroups of five batches
np chart of batches out of specification
u chart of viscosity per batch
Individuals and moving range chart
With one value per period and slow production, the ImR chart is the standard choice. Grouping five batches into a subgroup would mix days of production and delay any signal.
std
VI.A.3
An individuals chart has a mean of 12.0 and an average moving range of 0.60. Using E2 = 2.66, what are the control limits for the individuals?
Limits = X̄ ± E2·MR̄ = 12.0 ± 2.66 × 0.60 = 12.0 ± 1.60, so 10.40 to 13.60. Using 3 × MR̄ gives 10.20 to 13.80, which treats the moving range as if it were sigma.
std
VI.A.3
A shop chooses a median chart instead of an X̄-R chart for operators who chart by hand. What is the main trade-off?
It is simpler to plot but somewhat less sensitive to shifts in the mean
It is more sensitive to shifts in the mean but needs a computer to calculate
It removes the need for both a range chart and any control chart constants
It works only for attribute data that operators count by hand at the line

Operators can plot the middle value without calculating an average, which suits manual charting, but the median uses the data less efficiently than the mean, so small shifts are detected less readily. A range is still used to set the limits.
std
VI.A.3
A median chart uses subgroups of n = 5. The average of the subgroup medians is 10.00 and R̄ is 1.00. Using the median chart factor Ã2 = 0.691, what is the upper control limit?
UCL = average median + Ã2·R̄ = 10.00 + 0.691 × 1.00 = 10.69. Using the X̄ chart factor A2 = 0.577 gives 10.58, which is too narrow for medians.
std
VI.A.3
Each day an inspector checks every unit in a lot for any defect and records it as good or defective. Daily lot sizes vary from 120 to 300. Which chart fits best?
np chart
c chart
p chart
u chart

The data are counts of defective units with a changing sample size, which calls for a p chart of the proportion defective. An np chart needs a constant sample size, and c and u charts count defects rather than defective units.
std
VI.A.3
A p chart uses samples of n = 150 and the average proportion defective is 0.04. What are the control limits?
UCL 0.628, LCL 0
UCL 0.088, LCL 0
σp = √(0.04 × 0.96 / 150) = 0.016, so UCL = 0.04 + 0.048 = 0.088; the computed LCL is negative, so it is set to 0. Leaving the LCL at −0.008 is a common slip, since a proportion cannot be below zero.
std
VI.A.3
A team inspects exactly 50 connectors from each shift, records the number of defective connectors, and wants operators to plot the count directly. Which chart should they use?
p chart
np chart
c chart
X̄-R chart

With a constant sample size, the number of defective units can be plotted as a count on an np chart, which operators find easy. A p chart would also work but requires converting to a proportion, which is not what they want.
std
VI.A.3
An np chart uses a constant sample of n = 200 and the average proportion defective is 0.05. What are the control limits?
UCL 19.25, LCL 0

n·p̄ = 10 and σ = √(10 × 0.95) = 3.08, so the limits are 10 ± 9.25, or 0.75 to 19.25. Using √(n·p̄) treats the data as Poisson (c chart) and gives 0.51 to 19.49, and the LCL is positive here, so it is not set to 0.
std
VI.A.3
Painted door panels of the same size are checked, and the number of paint blemishes on each panel is recorded. Which chart fits best?
p chart
np chart
c chart
ImR chart
Counting defects on an inspection unit of constant size calls for a c chart. The p and np charts count defective units, which would lose the information about how many blemishes each panel has.
std
VI.A.3
A c chart for flaws per casting has an average of 9 flaws. What are the control limits?
UCL 36, LCL 0
UCL 12, LCL 6
UCL 18, LCL 0
UCL 15, LCL 3
UCL = c̄ + 3√c̄ = 9 + 9 = 18 and LCL = 9 − 9 = 0. Multiplying c̄ itself by 3 gives 36, and ±√c̄ alone gives 1-sigma limits of 6 to 12.
std
VI.A.3
Fabric rolls of different lengths are inspected, and the number of weaving flaws on each roll is counted. Which chart should be used?
c chart
u chart
np chart
p chart
Defect counts from inspection units of varying size need a u chart, which plots defects per unit (here per meter) so rolls can be compared. A c chart assumes every roll is the same size.
std
VI.A.3
A u chart tracks defects per circuit board. Each sample has 8 boards, and the average is 2.0 defects per board. What are the control limits?
UCL 6.2, LCL 0
UCL 3.5, LCL 0.5
UCL 2.8, LCL 1.3
UCL 2.5, LCL 1.5
σu = √(ū/n) = √(2.0/8) = 0.5, so the limits are 2.0 ± 1.5, or 0.5 to 3.5. Leaving out n gives √2.0 = 1.41 and limits of 0 to 6.2, far too wide for samples of 8 boards.
std
VI.A.3
On a new X̄-R chart, the R chart has two points above its upper limit while the X̄ chart looks in control. What should the analyst do first?
Read the X̄ chart alone, because it is the chart that shows the process mean
Treat the R chart points as noise, since the averages on the X̄ chart are stable
Resolve the R chart signals, because the X̄ limits are based on R̄
Widen both sets of limits so they include the two high ranges

The X̄ limits are calculated from R̄, so an unstable range makes them unreliable; the R chart should be brought into control first. Reading the X̄ chart on its own assumes limits that the R chart has just called into question.
std
VI.A.3
A Green Belt's project cut the spread of a process, and the chart now shows many points crowded near the center line. When should the control limits be recalculated?
After the change is confirmed and enough stable data are collected
Each month, so the limits reflect the latest data
Never, because the original limits are the baseline for the process
Whenever a point falls outside the limits and the cause is unclear

Limits should be revised after a deliberate, verified process change, using enough new in-control data. Recalculating whenever a point goes out hides real signals, and recalculating on a fixed calendar does the same with slow drifts.
std
VI.A.3
A supervisor draws the part's specification limits on an X̄ chart in place of the control limits. Why is this a problem?
Specification limits are tighter than control limits for a capable process
Specification limits belong on attribute control charts instead
Specification limits apply to individual parts, not to subgroup averages
Specification limits must be recalculated from the data every week

Averages vary less than individual values, so averages can sit well inside the specification while many single parts are out, and the chart no longer reflects the process's own variation. Specification limits are set by the customer, not calculated from data.
std
VI.B.1
A draft control plan lists each characteristic, its specification, the gauge, and the sample size and frequency. Which addition is most important before the plan is released?
The names of the project team members who wrote it
A history of the project's analysis and improvement work
The cost savings the project is expected to deliver
A reaction plan for when a check fails

The reaction plan tells the operator what to do with the process and the product when a check is out of control or out of specification, which is what makes the plan work on the floor. Team names and savings belong in project records, not in the control plan.
std
VI.B.1
A Green Belt is helping write a control plan for an improved process. Which characteristics should it focus on?
Every dimension on the drawing, each given equal attention in the plan
Only the final outputs that the customer inspects at its receiving dock
Those characteristics that are easiest to measure on the line
The key inputs and outputs shown to drive the results in the project

The plan should control the critical X's and Y's found in analysis and confirmed in improvement, often ranked through the FMEA. Controlling only final outputs reacts after the fact and misses the inputs that caused the problem.
std
VI.B.1
The project is closing, and the control plan is ready. What is the most important step in implementing it?
File it with the project documents so auditors can find it
Give it to the process owner, train its users, and verify it is followed
Post it in the break room so the operators on every shift can read it
Email it to the plant manager for review at the next quarterly meeting

A control plan only sustains gains if the process owner accepts it, the people doing the checks are trained, and its use is verified. Filing or posting it creates a record but does not make anyone carry it out.
std
VI.B.1
A year after a project, the process gets a new fixture and the FMEA is updated with a new failure mode. What should happen to the control plan?
It should stay as written, since it reflects the project's final state
It should be replaced by the updated FMEA, which now covers the same content
It should be revised to cover the change, because it is a living document
It should be withdrawn, since the project is closed and its gains are secured

A control plan documents how the current process is monitored, so it is updated whenever the process, the FMEA or the measurement methods change. Leaving it frozen at project close means the new risk goes unmonitored.
std
VI.B.2
Months after a project, an operator is found using a printed work instruction with the old machine settings. Which document control weakness does this most directly show?
The work instruction was written in too much detail
The operator was not shown the project's charter
The document did not list the project team's names
Obsolete copies were not withdrawn or marked
Document control must keep current, approved versions at the point of use and prevent the use of obsolete ones. Too much detail or a missing charter would not cause old settings to be used.
std
VI.B.2
After a project changes the setup procedure, the team plans to email the new steps to the operators. Why should the change go through document control instead?
Only the approved, current version stays in use, so the gain holds
Document control makes the project easier to close on schedule
Document control removes the need to train the operators on the change
It allows each operator to keep a personal copy with their own notes

Running the change through document control gives it review, approval, a revision level and controlled distribution, so people keep working to the improved method. Email copies multiply uncontrolled versions, and controlled documents still require training.
std
VI.B.2
An engineer wants to change a temperature setpoint in a controlled procedure. What is the correct path?
Mark up the posted copy by hand and tell each of the shift leads about it
Change the electronic file directly but keep the same revision level on it
Get it reviewed and approved, issue the new revision, withdraw the old one
Wait until the annual review of all procedures and change it then

Controlled changes are reviewed and approved, the revision is identified, the new version is distributed and the old one removed from use. Handwritten edits and silent changes leave no approval or revision history.
std
VI.B.3
A new assembly method will roll out to three shifts. What should come first when developing the training plan?
Book a classroom and schedule a single session for all three shifts
Write a quiz that operators must pass at the end of the training
Ask the supplier of the new fixture to run the training sessions
Identify who needs training and what skills they lack

A training plan starts with a needs analysis: who is affected and what skills they must gain. Scheduling sessions or writing tests before knowing the audience and gaps risks training the wrong people on the wrong content.
std
VI.B.3
When is the best time to train operators on a new standard work sequence?
Several months ahead, so they have time to absorb the method
Just before go-live, hands-on, with the new instructions
After go-live, once problems show where training is needed
Only when an operator asks for help with the new method

Training close to go-live, using the actual approved instructions and real practice, gives the best retention and avoids teaching a draft. Training long in advance is forgotten, and training after problems appear lets defects reach the process first.
std
VI.B.3
Six months after a successful project, newly hired operators are making the errors the project had eliminated. What was most likely missing from the training plan?
Adding the new method to onboarding and refresher training
Training the original operators before the go-live date
A written test for each of the project team members
A sign-in sheet for each of the training sessions held
Sustaining gains needs the new method built into ongoing training, especially for new hires and periodic refreshers. Training only the original crew works at go-live but fades as people change.
std
VI.B.3
How should a Green Belt judge whether training on the improved process has been effective?
Count the number of people who signed the attendance sheet
Ask attendees whether they enjoyed the training session
Observe the work and check that the process results have held
Compare the training hours with the hours in the original plan
Effective training shows up as correct behavior on the job and sustained process results. Attendance and satisfaction measure activity, not whether the improvement is being carried out.
std
VI.B.4
A company's own trained staff audit its warehouse against the company's procedures. What type of audit is this?
First-party audit
Second-party audit
Third-party audit
Certification audit
An audit an organization performs on itself is a first-party (internal) audit. A second-party audit is performed by a customer or other interested party on a supplier.
std
VI.B.4
A manufacturer hires an independent consultant to audit its own processes before a customer visit. What type of audit is the consultant's?
First-party audit
Second-party audit
Third-party audit
Supplier audit

An audit done by or on behalf of the organization itself is first-party, even when an outside person carries it out. Using an external auditor does not make it third-party, which is done by an independent body such as a registrar.
std
VI.B.4
An automaker sends its quality engineer to audit a supplier's plant. What type of audit is this?
First-party audit
Second-party audit
Third-party audit
Internal quality audit
A customer auditing its supplier is a second-party audit. It is not third-party, because the customer has an interest in the outcome rather than being independent.
std
VI.B.4
A certification body audits a company's management system to decide whether to grant certification. What type of audit is this?
First-party audit
Second-party audit
Third-party audit
Process audit
A third-party audit is conducted by an independent organization, such as a registrar, with no stake in the result. A process audit describes scope, not who performs the audit.
std
VI.B.5
A team studies a sealing problem, finds the likely cause, sets a target, and chooses a countermeasure to try. Which PDCA step is this?
Plan
Do
Check
Act
Defining the problem, analyzing causes, setting the goal and choosing what to change is all Plan. Do begins when the chosen change is actually tried.
std
VI.B.5
The team runs the new sealing settings on one line for two weeks while collecting data. Which PDCA step is this?
Plan
Do
Check
Act
Do carries out the planned change, preferably on a small scale, and collects data. Check comes next, when the results are compared with the prediction.
std
VI.B.5
The team compares the pilot's leak rate with its target and with the baseline. Which PDCA step is this?
Plan
Do
Check
Act
Check (also called Study) compares the results with what was predicted and with the baseline. Act is the decision that follows, such as standardizing the change.
std
VI.B.5
The pilot met its target, so the team updates the work instructions and rolls the settings out to every line. Which PDCA step is this?
Plan
Do
Check
Act
Act standardizes a change that worked, through documents, training and controls, or starts a new cycle if it did not. Do is the small-scale trial, not the full rollout of a proven change.
std
VI.B.5
A pilot cut the defect rate by only a third of what the team predicted. What is the best next step under PDCA?
Standardize the change anyway, since it gave some improvement
Drop the project, since the countermeasure did not meet its target
Use what was learned to plan another cycle with a revised change
Skip the next Check step and roll out to all lines to save time

PDCA is iterative: in Act, a change that falls short is not standardized as-is; its lessons feed a new Plan. Abandoning the effort wastes what was learned, and standardizing a partial fix locks in a weak solution.
std
VI.C.1
In TPM, operators cleaning, inspecting and lubricating their own machines each day is known as:
Planned maintenance
Predictive maintenance
Autonomous maintenance
Corrective maintenance
Autonomous maintenance gives operators routine care of their equipment so small problems are found early. Planned maintenance is the scheduled work done by the maintenance staff.
std
VI.C.1
A plant measures bearing vibration weekly and replaces each bearing when its vibration trend shows wear, rather than on a fixed schedule. What type of maintenance is this?
Preventive maintenance
Breakdown maintenance
Autonomous maintenance
Predictive maintenance
Predictive (condition-based) maintenance uses measured condition, such as vibration, to act just before failure. Preventive maintenance acts on a fixed time or usage interval regardless of condition.
std
VI.C.1
A project cut diameter variation by restoring worn spindles on a lathe. How can TPM best help keep this gain?
Add spindle checks with a condition limit to routine maintenance
Wait for the control chart to show a problem, then rebuild the spindle
Replace the lathe with a new machine once the project closes
Move the lathe to the least busy cell so the spindle wears more slowly

Building the critical equipment condition into routine maintenance keeps the cause of the improvement in place, so the process stays in control. Waiting for the chart to signal means defects are already being made.
std
VI.C.1
A machine runs with 90% availability, 95% performance efficiency and 98% quality rate. What is its overall equipment effectiveness (OEE)?
OEE = availability × performance × quality = 0.90 × 0.95 × 0.98 = 0.838, or 83.8%. Averaging the three factors gives 94.3%, which understates the combined losses.
std
VI.C.1
Which statement best describes the aim of TPM?
Involve all employees in equipment care, aiming at zero breakdowns
Have maintenance staff handle every equipment task to free operators for production
Replace equipment on a fixed age so it never reaches the end of its life
Shift all maintenance to outside contractors to lower the fixed cost

TPM is a company-wide approach that involves operators, maintenance and management in maximizing equipment effectiveness, with zero breakdowns and zero defects as goals. Keeping all care with maintenance staff is the traditional model TPM moves away from.
std
VI.C.2
Shadow boards for tools, painted floor lanes and status boards at each cell share which main purpose?
Make normal and abnormal conditions obvious at a glance
Make the shop floor look neat and tidy for customer visits
Replace written procedures and operator training on the line
Track each operator's individual output during the shift
Visual factory elements let anyone see at once whether things are as they should be, so problems are spotted and fixed quickly. They support, but do not replace, documented procedures and training.
std
VI.C.2
An assembler finds a missing part and pulls a cord, which lights a lamp over her station and calls the team leader. What is this device called?
Kanban
Andon
Poka-yoke
Heijunka
An andon is a visual or audible signal that calls attention to a problem so help arrives quickly. Kanban signals replenishment of material, not an abnormal condition.
std
VI.C.2
A press has a sensor that detects a double blank and stops the press automatically before the next stroke. Which principle does this show?
Kaizen
Takt time
Jidoka
Heijunka

Jidoka (autonomation) builds in the ability to detect an abnormality and stop automatically, so defects are not passed on and one person can watch several machines. Takt time is the pace of customer demand, not a stopping rule.
std
VI.C.2
On a line, a machine stops itself when it detects a fault and a tower light turns red. Which statement correctly separates jidoka from andon here?
Jidoka is the automatic stop, and andon is the light
Jidoka is the light, and andon is the automatic stop
Both describe the same device and can be used interchangeably
Andon applies only to people, so neither term fits this machine
Jidoka is the principle of stopping when an abnormality is detected, and andon is the signal that makes the stop visible so help comes. The two often work together but are not the same thing.
std
VI.C.2
After a project sets a new pressure window for a hydraulic system, how can visual controls best help hold the gain?
Post the project's final report on the bulletin board near the system
Ask operators to memorize the new pressure values for the system
Keep the new values in a binder in the supervisor's office for reference
Mark the gauge face with green and red zones for the new window

Marking the acceptable range right on the gauge makes an out-of-window reading obvious to anyone at the point of use. Posting reports or keeping values in a binder depends on people looking for information away from the process.
std
